anchor_text: make a Star Chamber matter
summary: The Star Chamber was a powerful royal court that sat at Westminster without a jury and handled cases of riot, disorder, and crimes by powerful men who could intimidate ordinary courts. Shallow threatens to take his complaint against Falstaff to this highest level of English law — signaling that he considers the offense serious and expects the council's authority to override local justice.
detail: The Court of Star Chamber (named for the starred ceiling of the room at Westminster where it met) operated from the late fifteenth century and was formally organized under Henry VII. By Shakespeare's day it was used to punish riots, maintenance (using influence to pervert justice), perjury, and similar offenses beyond local remedy. It was both feared and respected as the council's judicial arm. Shallow invoking it in the opening line immediately sets up his pomposity: a country justice threatening London's highest court over a poaching incident in Windsor.

sources.name: Baker, Introduction to English Legal History
sources.citation: J. H. Baker, An Introduction to English Legal History, 4th ed. (2002), ch. 8 (the Court of Star Chamber and its jurisdiction).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1

Baker's Introduction to English Legal History is a real and standard work; the Star Chamber is covered in the chapter on conciliar courts, and all substantive claims about its jurisdiction and composition are accurate.

The Star Chamber explanation is accurate and directly supported by the text; Shallow's threat in line 1 is the opening beat of his pomposity, and the annotation's characterization of his escalation is mainstream and sound.

anchor_text: dozen white luces in their coat
summary: A 'luce' is a full-grown freshwater pike (from Latin 'lucius'). Shallow claims his family coat of arms bears a dozen white luces — a pointed dig at a real Warwickshire family, the Lucys of Charlecote, whose arms bore luces and who may have prosecuted the young Shakespeare for poaching. Evans mishears 'luces' as 'louses' (lice), which is part of the joke: the fish that marks Shallow's heraldic dignity becomes vermin in the Welsh parson's mouth.
detail: The Lucy family of Charlecote Park, near Stratford, bore three luces (pike) in their coat of arms. A longstanding tradition holds that Shakespeare was caught poaching on Lucy land and satirized him as Justice Shallow. Whether or not the biographical story is true, the wordplay is deliberate: 'louse' and 'luce' were phonetically close enough for Evans's Welsh-accented confusion to land. Evans then adds that lice 'signifies love' — an absurd folk-etymology that undercuts Shallow's heraldic pride. The 'old coat' is both the worn heraldic garment and the antiquity of the family; the salt fish joke ('the salt fish is an old coat') is Shallow's contemptuous counter.

The luce/louse pun (lines 14-17) is explicitly performed in the text and the Lucy-of-Charlecote biographical tradition is correctly flagged as unverified tradition rather than fact; marking confidence 'medium' is appropriate caution.

anchor_text: I may quarter, coz
summary: Slender asks whether he can 'quarter' the coat of arms — a heraldic term meaning to combine two family crests in one shield (which happens when a gentleman marries an heiress). Shallow confirms he may do so by marrying Anne Page. Evans's reply ('It is marring indeed') mishears 'marrying' as 'marring' (damaging), turning a proud heraldic ambition into a warning about ruin — because 'if he quarter it' he would only have three-quarters left for himself.
detail: Quartering a coat of arms by marriage was a mark of social advancement: the groom's arms and the bride's family arms were divided into quarters on the same shield. Evans's Welsh pronunciation collapses 'marrying' into 'marring' (ruining), producing a comic non-sequitur that accidentally captures what the whole Slender-Anne subplot will prove — that this match is indeed a kind of 'marring' for Slender, who ends up eloping with a disguised boy.

The heraldic meaning of 'quarter' and Evans's marrying/marring pun are both textually confirmed (lines 18-23) and the annotation does not over-read the subplot outcome as prophetic commentary — it notes it as comic non-sequitur that accidentally anticipates events.

anchor_text: no fear of Got in a riot
summary: 'Got' is Evans's Welsh-accented pronunciation of 'God.' Evans argues that the Privy Council (he calls it 'the Council') will want to hear a matter involving 'the fear of God' — meaning godly conduct and reverence — not a common brawl. 'Vizaments' (from French 'avisement') means considered judgment or prudent advice: he is urging Shallow to think carefully before escalating to the Council. The dialect is comic but Evans's point is reasonable.
detail: Welsh speakers typically voiced the unvoiced dental fricative, producing 'Got' for 'God,' 'goot' for 'good,' 'petter' for 'better,' 'py'r lady' for 'by Our Lady.' These features are consistent throughout Evans's speeches and would have been immediately recognizable as stage-Welsh to an Elizabethan audience. The comedy does not undercut Evans's function: he is repeatedly the voice of moderation and community peace in this scene.

anchor_text: pribbles and prabbles
summary: 'Pribbles and prabbles' is Evans's Welsh-inflected phrase for petty squabbles or trivial disputes — effectively 'bickering and quarreling.' It is a comic reduplication (like 'dilly-dallying'), not a standard English word, and appears only in Shakespeare, probably as a parody of Welsh speech patterns. Evans is urging everyone to drop these small grievances and consider the marriage proposal instead.
detail: The reduplication with front-vowel variation ('pribble-prabble') mimics a common pattern in colloquial English intensifiers; Shakespeare gives Evans several such formations ('prains' for brains, etc.). The word appears to be Shakespeare's own coinage, not a documented dialect term, though it cleverly sounds both Welsh and childish — perfect for a parson urging adults to behave.

Glossing 'pribbles and prabbles' as petty squabbles and identifying it as an apparent Shakespearean coinage is sound; the note that it 'appears to be' coined rather than asserting it definitively is appropriate.

anchor_text: by yea and no, I do
summary: 'By yea and no' was the typical oath-form associated with Puritan and Quaker sensibility, based on Matthew 5:37 — Jesus's command not to swear at all, but to 'let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay.' Shallow is marking himself as a plain, godly gentleman who swears simply and honestly. The oath crops up frequently in the play around Shallow and Page, locating them as sober Windsor citizens.
detail: The Sermon on the Mount's prohibition on oaths ('Swear not at all... but let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay; for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil,' Matthew 5:34-37 Geneva 1599) was a touchstone for godly Elizabethan Protestants and radical reformers. 'By yea and no' thus signals a middle-class, godly Windsor world quite unlike the courtly and military world Falstaff inhabits.

anchor_text: Pauca verba, Sir John; goot worts
summary: 'Pauca verba' is Latin for 'few words' — Evans is telling Falstaff to say less and keep the peace. Falstaff immediately mocks Evans's Welsh mispronunciation of 'words' as 'worts' (a wort is a plant, especially a pot-herb or cabbage): he pretends to hear Evans say 'good cabbages.' The pun deflates Evans's pompous Latin by turning it into kitchen-garden nonsense.
detail: The Latin tag 'pauca verba' (or 'pauca') was a common colloquial tag in Elizabethan English, used the way 'in short' or 'enough said' might be today; it recurs in other Shakespeare plays (2 Henry IV). Falstaff's 'Good worts! good cabbage!' is purely comic deflation: he refuses to engage the substance of Evans's peace-making by turning the dialect into a vegetable-joke.

anchor_text: cony-catching rascals
summary: 'Cony-catching' meant swindling or cheating — a 'cony' (rabbit) being slang for a naive victim easily snared. The term was made famous by a series of popular pamphlets by Robert Greene in the 1590s exposing the tricks of London con-men ('A Notable Discovery of Coosnage,' 1591, etc.). Slender calls Bardolph, Nym, and Pistol 'cony-catching rascals' because they picked his pocket while getting him drunk — textbook cony-catching.
detail: Robert Greene's 'cony-catching' pamphlets catalogued the underworld cant and confidence tricks of Elizabethan London's criminal milieu; the term became instantly recognizable shorthand for petty fraud and trickery. Slender's use of the fashionable term (he has probably read the pamphlets, or heard them discussed) is mildly comic coming from such a guileless figure.

anchor_text: You Banbury cheese
summary: Banbury, a town in Oxfordshire, was famous for a thin, dry, crumbly cheese roughly an inch thick. Bardolph calls the skinny Slender a 'Banbury cheese' as an insult meaning he is thin, insubstantial, and easy to dismiss. The taunt suits Slender perfectly — he is slight, tentative, and offers no resistance.
detail: Banbury cheese was proverbially thin — a common Elizabethan byword for leanness, the wafer-like round left when the rind was pared away. Bardolph's one-line insult is the scene's funniest verbal economy: Slender's helpless response ('Ay, it is no matter') makes him seem even more like an obliging rind of cheese — flat and harmless.

anchor_text: How now, Mephostophilus
summary: Mephostophilus (Mephistopheles) is the devil who serves Doctor Faustus in Marlowe's play 'Doctor Faustus' (c. 1592), which was enormously popular in London and still being performed when Shakespeare wrote 'The Merry Wives.' Pistol calls Slender by the devil's name as a mock-threatening insult — a bit of bluster that only emphasizes how harmless Slender actually is.
detail: Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (c. 1592, printed 1604 and 1616) made Mephistopheles one of the most recognizable figures in the popular repertory; audiences would have caught the reference immediately. Pistol's bombastic style is full of such theatrical allusions — he speaks in scraps of old plays and heroic posturing. Calling the timid Slender 'Mephostophilus' is the kind of wildly disproportionate threat that defines Pistol's character.

Pistol calling Slender 'Mephostophilus' (line 100) as a theatrical allusion to Marlowe's Faustus demon is mainstream, and the reading of it as wildly disproportionate bluster defining Pistol's character is the standard interpretation.

anchor_text: That's my humour
summary: Nym's catchword 'humour' (he uses it throughout the play) parodies a fashion in Elizabethan writing and speech — particularly associated with Ben Jonson's 'comical humours' plays, where characters are dominated by a single ruling passion or affectation. Nym applies the word to almost any situation, drained of real meaning, as a tic of fashionable slang that makes him sound ridiculous rather than menacing.
detail: The medical theory of 'humours' (the four bodily fluids — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile — whose balance determined temperament) had been turned into a literary fashion, especially by Ben Jonson's Every Man In His Humour (1598) and Every Man Out of His Humour (1599). Nym's mantra 'that is my humour' or 'that is the humour of it' empties the fashionable word of content — it becomes a verbal filler, a swagger-word. Shakespeare is gently satirizing the humour-craze.

sources.name: Jonson, Every Man In His Humour (1598)
sources.citation: Ben Jonson, Every Man In His Humour (1598) and Every Man Out of His Humour (1599): the literary vogue for 'humour' characters that Nym parodies.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 102

Jonson's Every Man In His Humour (performed 1598) and Every Man Out of His Humour (performed 1599) are real plays, and the humours-fashion satire they represent is the standard scholarly context for Nym's catchword.

Nym's repeated 'that's my humour' (line 102) as a parody of the Jonsonian humours fashion is a well-established reading, and the annotation correctly stops short of claiming direct parody of a specific Jonson play rather than a general craze.

anchor_text: seven groats in mill-sixpences, and two Edward shovel-boards
summary: Slender itemizes exactly what was stolen with the fussy precision of a man who keeps count of small change. 'Groats' were four-penny coins; 'mill-sixpences' were sixpences made by the newer milling process (smoother edges, harder to clip). 'Shovel-boards' were large, heavy old coins — typically broad shillings from the reign of Edward VI — used as playing-pieces in the pub game of shovelboard (shove-penny). Slender's detailed inventory makes him both comic and sympathetic.
detail: The shovelboard game involved pushing coins along a long table to land in a scoring zone; old wide shillings were ideal pieces. 'Edward shovel-boards' are coins from Edward VI's reign (1547-53), already old by the play's date. Mill-sixpences, made by a horse-powered rolling mill introduced around 1561, had cleaner edges than hammered coins and were thus harder to clip (shave for silver). Slender's mix of penny-counting and pub-gaming perfectly characterises his modest, uncourtly world.

The identification of groats, mill-sixpences, and Edward shovel-boards (lines 116-119) is accurate in every material detail, and the characterization of Slender's petty inventory as comic yet sympathetic is a defensible mainstream reading.

anchor_text: latten bilbo ... Word of denial in thy labras
summary: Pistol's pompous threat to Evans is a jumble of swagger-words. A 'bilbo' is a fine Spanish sword (from Bilbao, famous for its steel); 'latten' is a copper-zinc alloy resembling brass — so a 'latten bilbo' is a flashy-looking but cheap sword, fitting for Pistol's empty bluster. 'Labras' is a Hispanicism for lips (Spanish 'labras' / 'labios'), part of the theatrical soldier's foreign-word posturing.
detail: Bilbao (Bilbo) blades were celebrated for their flexible temper — a genuine bilbo was a fine weapon. Calling Evans 'this latten bilbo' implies he is a sham knight, bright on the surface but made of base metal. 'Mountain-foreigner' is Pistol's contemptuous name for the Welshman Evans. Pistol's speeches are pastiches of the ranting braggart-soldier style popular on the Elizabethan stage, full of half-remembered military foreign words and inflated cadences from old bombastic plays.

anchor_text: marry trap with you, if you run the nuthook's humour on me
summary: 'Marry trap' was an exclamation meaning 'gotcha' or 'caught you!' — it appears to have been used when someone fell into a trick. A 'nuthook' was a hooked stick for pulling down nut-laden branches, and also slang for a constable or catch-pole (a bailiff who hooks people in for arrest). Nym is warning Slender: if you try to arrest or trap me on this accusation, I'll turn it back on you. Characteristically, he adds 'that is the very note of it' — another meaningless tag-phrase.
detail: The exact idiom 'marry trap' is obscure, but context makes clear it is a retort or come-back phrase. 'Nuthook' as slang for a constable or petty officer was current in Elizabethan English — Mistress Quickly uses it in 2 Henry IV. Nym's warning combines legal-sounding aggression with his typical empty affectations, reinforcing his character as all style and no substance.

anchor_text: What say you, Scarlet and John
summary: Falstaff addresses Bardolph and Nym (or Pistol) as 'Scarlet and John' — a glancing reference to Will Scarlet and Little John, the most famous of Robin Hood's merry men. The nickname fits Bardolph perfectly: Will Scarlet was known for his fiery red face, and Bardolph's crimson nose and cheeks are a running joke throughout the Falstaff plays.
detail: Robin Hood and his outlaws were subjects of popular ballads, plays, and May Games across England. Associating Falstaff's gang with Robin Hood's crew is partly self-flattery on Falstaff's part — outlaws living outside the law by wit and good fellowship — and partly a joke at Bardolph's expense, since 'Scarlet' mocks his inflamed complexion. The allusion ties into the As You Like It world of greenwood outlaws that the Elizabethan stage loved.

anchor_text: being fap, sir, was, as they say, cashier'd; and so conclusions passed the careires
summary: 'Fap' means drunk. 'Cashiered' normally means discharged from service, but Bardolph uses it here to mean Slender was rendered helpless (his wallet discharged of its contents). 'Careires' (careers) is from horsemanship — a full gallop, or a charge. Bardolph is pretending to give a legal account of events ('conclusions passed the careires' = the outcome went at a gallop, i.e. things moved too fast for Slender to follow), but is actually just stringing together impressive-sounding words as an excuse.
detail: Evans's sharp correction — 'It is his five senses; fie, what the ignorance is!' — catches Bardolph's more obvious blunder of saying 'five sentences' for 'five senses.' But the whole speech is bluster. 'Fap' as drunk is recorded almost exclusively in this passage; 'careires' was technical equestrian vocabulary applied metaphorically. Bardolph's garbled account mirrors Slender's garbled legal Latin earlier in the scene — the play is full of people misusing technical vocabularies they barely understand.

anchor_text: I had rather than forty shillings I had my Book of Songs and Sonnets here
summary: The 'Book of Songs and Sonnets' is Tottel's Miscellany (1557), a famous anthology of English love poetry — the first printed collection of its kind in England, containing poems by Wyatt, Surrey, and others. That Slender's idea of wooing is to read aloud from a printed poetry anthology rather than speak for himself is the joke: he is so unequipped for courtship that he needs a book of borrowed love-talk.
detail: Richard Tottel's Songes and Sonettes (1557), known as Tottel's Miscellany, went through many editions and was still in circulation in the 1590s. It was the era's most popular anthology of courtly love verse. Slender's wish for it — instead of his absent servant and in the presence of Anne Page — perfectly captures his helplessness: he cannot improvise a single spontaneous word of affection and hopes a published text will do the work for him.

anchor_text: Alice Shortcake upon Allhallowmas last, a fortnight afore Michaelmas
summary: Simple points out the impossibility of Slender's claim by citing two fixed church holidays: Allhallowmas (All Saints' Day, 1 November) and Michaelmas (Feast of St Michael, 29 September). A fortnight (two weeks) before Michaelmas would be around 15 September — which comes before 1 November, not after it. Simple has caught Slender in a chronological absurdity, which Slender does not even notice.
detail: Both Allhallowmas and Michaelmas were quarter-days in the English calendar — standard dates for settling accounts, renewing leases, and marking the passage of the farming year. The joke requires the audience to know their sequence: Michaelmas (29 September) comes before Allhallowmas (1 November), so lending a book 'last Allhallowmas' and receiving it back 'a fortnight before Michaelmas' is impossible. Simple's pedantic correction is funnier because Slender ignores it.

anchor_text: three veneys for a dish of stewed prunes
summary: A 'veney' (or 'venue,' from French) is a hit or bout in fencing — Slender bruised his shin playing three bouts of sword-and-dagger against a fencing-master for a wager of stewed prunes. 'Stewed prunes' had a bawdy association (they were served in brothels), but Slender is almost certainly too naive to intend the pun — he simply means a dish of prunes as a prize, which is itself absurd (risking injury for fruit).
detail: Fencing masters held public schools and challenge matches; paying for bouts with food was a mock-wager form. 'Stewed prunes' were proverbially associated with brothels in Elizabethan London — they were thought to prevent venereal disease. Slender's choice of prize adds an inadvertent layer of comedy: he has risked a bruised shin to win a brothel-associated food item, entirely unaware of any implications. The phrase 'I cannot abide the smell of hot meat since' compounds the effect.

anchor_text: I have seen Sackerson loose twenty times
summary: Sackerson was a real, famous bear kept at the Paris Garden bear-baiting arena in Southwark, London — the same neighborhood as the Globe Theatre. Bear-baiting was a hugely popular Elizabethan sport in which chained bears were set upon by dogs. Sackerson is name-checked by Slender as a proof of his own bravery: he has watched the famous bear loose from his chain twenty times without flinching. The detail grounds the play firmly in a recognizable London entertainment culture.
detail: The Paris Garden (and the adjacent Bear Garden at Bankside) were licensed bear-baiting venues operating alongside the public theatres across the Thames from the City. Named bears like Sackerson and Harry Hunks were celebrity animals; Philip Henslowe's diary records bear-keepers and their animals by name. Slender's boast about Sackerson is a comic exercise in misplaced courage — he is terrified of wooing Anne Page but is proud to have stood near a famous bear.

Sackerson as a real documented bear at the Paris Garden bear-baiting arena is confirmed by Henslowe's records, and reading Slender's bear-courage boast as comic contrast with his terror of wooing Anne Page is the standard and fully defensible interpretation.

anchor_text: By cock and pie
summary: 'By cock and pie' was a mild oath, a softened form of 'by God and the pyx (the liturgical vessel for the eucharistic bread).' The 'cock' is a common corruption of 'God' used to avoid direct swearing; the 'pie' is the ordinal or table of church services (a complex liturgical reference guide used before the Reformation). It signals Windsor's bluff, unpretentious, countryman piety — swearing by something religious but in a comfortably softened form.
detail: Elizabethan mild oaths typically substituted near-homophones for sacred names to sidestep blasphemy while preserving the force of emphasis: 'cock' for 'God,' 'pie' for the Catholic pie (the index to the old service-books). By the Reformation, 'cock and pie' had become a rustic catch-phrase drained of most doctrinal content.

sources.name: OED s.v. cock and pie

The analysis of 'by cock and pie' as a softened oath substituting 'cock' for 'God' and 'pie' for the liturgical ordinal is standard, and attributing it to Page's bluff countryman register is appropriate given who speaks it at line 227.

anchor_text: his dry nurse, or his cook
summary: A 'dry nurse' cared for a young child without breastfeeding — managing feeding, washing, and watching — as distinct from a 'wet nurse' who suckled an infant. Evans is piling up Mistress Quickly's domestic roles (nurse, cook, laundress, wringer) to convey that she does everything in Doctor Caius's household.
detail: The wet nurse / dry nurse distinction was standard Elizabethan household language. A wet nurse supplied breast milk to an infant whose mother could not or would not suckle; a dry nurse managed all the physical care of an older child or the non-feeding care of an infant. By Evans's time the term could be applied loosely to any general household caretaker of a gentleman's domestic affairs. The comic list — nurse, dry nurse, cook, laundry, wringer — emphasizes Quickly's indispensable and multi-purpose role, while also signalling that Caius's French household is small and somewhat disorganized.

The wet-nurse/dry-nurse distinction and the reading of Evans's list as comic accumulation of domestic roles are accurate and mainstream; nothing overreaches.

anchor_text: his laundry, his washer, and his wringer
summary: 'Laundry' here means a laundress — a woman whose job is washing linen — not a room or building. A 'wringer' is one who physically wrings (twists) wet cloth to squeeze out the water, a separate step in hand-washing before wringing-machines existed. Evans's list of job-nouns treats Mistress Quickly as a one-woman domestic staff.
detail: In Elizabethan English 'laundry' could denote the person who launders as well as the place or act of laundering (OED distinguishes the agent sense, now obsolete). The sequence 'laundry, washer, wringer' breaks the washing process into three distinct tasks — soaking and rubbing, rinsing and washing, and finally wringing — each a named occupation in a larger household, here comic because Quickly does all three. Evans's Welsh formality inflates ordinary domestic labor into a dignified list, which is part of the scene's gentle humor.

The agent-sense of 'laundry' = laundress is well-attested, and the core joke of comic role-accumulation is sound; the claim that the three nouns map to three sequential washing steps slightly over-systematizes ('laundry' and 'washer' are closer to synonyms than distinct stages), but the overall interpretation is defensible.

anchor_text: desire and require her to solicit
summary: 'Desire and require' is a legal doublet — the pairing of near-synonyms to cover every shade of meaning, common in formal documents and ecclesiastical correspondence. Evans, as a Welsh parson, instinctively reaches for this church-legal register even when giving a servant a simple errand. The redundancy is part of his comic formality.
detail: Doublets in legal and ecclesiastical English — 'give and bequeath,' 'null and void,' 'cease and desist' — were standard formula intended to foreclose ambiguity between subtly different terms. 'Desire' implied a polite wish; 'require' carried authority or urgency; coupling them left no gap. Evans's use of the formula here to describe carrying a love-letter from Slender to Mistress Quickly is comically over-elaborate. The word 'solicit' in the same clause further inflates the register: it is the formal verb for legal or official petition. The joke is that the parson cannot turn off his clerical diction even in the most mundane commission.

sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'desire' vb. 3: 'to request'; s.v. 'require' vb. 2: 'to ask, request (with some degree of authority).' The pairing is standard in ecclesiastical petition language.

Identifying 'desire and require' as a legal-ecclesiastical doublet is mainstream; both terms appear in the same clause and the inflated-register joke is well-supported by the text and Evans's character as a parson.

anchor_text: pippins and cheese to come
summary: Pippins are a variety of apple — the name comes from the French 'pepin' (seed), applied to apples grown from seed rather than grafted. Cheese and apples eaten together was the standard Elizabethan dessert course; Evans is telling Simple he is interrupting his own after-dinner fruit-and-cheese course and must get back to it, grounding the play's opening moments in ordinary Windsor domestic life.
detail: Several varieties of pippin (Costard, Leather-coat, Golden) appear in Shakespeare; Falstaff asks for 'a pippin' at dinner in Henry IV Part 2 (5.3). The fruit and cheese pairing was a conventional close to meals across all social levels in Elizabethan England, widely mentioned in contemporary household books and recipe collections. Evans's mention of it is both a realistic domestic touch and a small indication that his Welsh parsimony — he is eating modestly at home, not at a tavern — is being disrupted by having to serve as Slender's matchmaking errand-runner.

anchor_text: bully rook? Speak scholarly and wisely
summary: The Host calls everyone 'bully' as a term of hearty affection (roughly 'fine fellow'), with no connection to modern bullying. A 'rook' is a cheat or swindler, but here used almost admiringly, as a term of swaggering comradeship. 'Speak scholarly and wisely' is mock-pompous encouragement, the Host performing a kind of comic ceremony around ordinary conversation.
detail: The Host's signature mode throughout the play is this extravagant slang: he addresses nearly every man he likes as 'bully,' sometimes adding a heroic epithet ('bully Hercules,' 'bully Hector,' 'bully Doctor,' 'bully stale'). The word derives from Dutch boel, a lover or fine fellow; in Elizabethan English it was a warm colloquialism with no sinister weight. 'Rook' as cheat or trickster was equally familiar slang (OED s.v. 'rook, n.2'). The Host's comically elevated diction throughout the scene — 'emperor, Caesar, Keiser, and Pheazar'; 'bully Hercules' — is part of his comic personality as an innkeeper who styles himself a ringmaster of large men.

anchor_text: Discard, bully Hercules; cashier; let them wag
summary: 'Cashier' means to dismiss a soldier from service, not to operate a cash register. The Host fires off three synonyms for sacking followers — 'discard,' 'cashier,' 'let them wag' (let them go) — in his usual style of rapid comic extravagance. Calling Falstaff 'bully Hercules' pairs the world's strongest mythological hero with a fat, broke knight who is struggling to pay his inn bill.

anchor_text: emperor, Caesar, Keiser, and Pheazar
summary: The Host strings together four words for 'ruler' as comic flattery for Falstaff, who is spending ten pounds a week at his inn. 'Caesar' is the Roman title; 'Keiser' is the German form (Kaiser, as in the Holy Roman Emperor); 'Pheazar' appears to be the Host's garbled version of 'vizier' (an Islamic minister of state) or simply a nonsense rhyme-word. The joke is the absurd escalation: innkeeper hails broke knight as the greatest rulers in the world.
detail: The Host's habit of rattling off grandiose titles and names ('bully Hercules,' 'bully Hector,' 'Caesar, Keiser, and Pheazar') is a form of comic hyperbole that deflates itself through excess. 'Pheazar' has puzzled editors: some read it as a variant of 'vizier' (via French visir), others as a nonce-word invented for the rhyme with 'Caesar' and 'Keiser.' Either way the joke works: the three words together represent East, West, and center of world empire, all deployed to flatter a man sitting in a Windsor inn. The irony is that Falstaff is, in fact, planning an empire of his own — a financial raid on two married women.

The gloss is accurate — 'Pheazar' as a comic nonce-rhyme or garbled 'vizier' is the standard editorial line, and the claim that the three titles represent world empire is defensible hyperbole-comedy reading, not over-reach.

anchor_text: froth and lime
summary: The Host instructs Bardolph in the two classic tricks of a dishonest tapster (under-bartender): 'froth' means to fill the cup with foam so it looks full when it is not, and 'lime' means to adulterate ale or wine with lime (calcium powder) to make cheap liquor appear stronger. Both were notorious frauds in Elizabethan taverns and subject to trade regulations.
detail: The Statute of Weights and Measures and borough by-laws regulated the sale of ale and wine; liming in particular was a recognized form of adulteration. Falstaff himself knows these tricks — in Henry IV Part 1 (2.4) he teases Bardolph as one who 'fills a pot of ale and safety.' The Host's laconic instruction here — 'I am at a word; follow' — accepts that a man like Bardolph, already practiced at petty theft in Falstaff's company, will need no further training in the art of cheating customers. Froth-building and liming are mentioned together in several Elizabethan trade complaints.

anchor_text: 'Convey' the wise it call. 'Steal!' foh! A fico for the phrase
summary: Pistol objects to the blunt word 'steal': the genteel euphemism is to 'convey' (carry away, transfer). 'A fico for the phrase' means 'damn the word' — a 'fico' (Italian for 'fig') was an obscene hand gesture made by thrusting the thumb between two fingers, used to express contempt. The joke is about the Elizabethan habit of using polite language to disguise theft.
detail: The 'conveyance' / 'convey' euphemism for theft was common enough to be satirized: 'convey' literally meant to carry or transfer property, but in criminal slang meant to steal. Pistol — who throughout the play speaks in bombastic, theatrical bluster — insists that his gang are too fine for the word 'steal' even as they plan to rob. The 'fico' or 'fig of Spain' was a well-known obscene gesture across Europe (compare Pistol's 'fig of Spain' in Henry V 3.6, and the Duke of York's 'Shall I be plain? I wish the bastards dead, / And I would have it suddenly performed. / I'll give a thousand pound to have it done... / Fig of Spain! The Duke of Gloucester' in 3 Henry VI). The gesture is explicitly glossed in several contemporary pamphlets as Italian in origin.

anchor_text: hath a legion of angels
summary: An 'angel' was a gold coin worth about ten shillings, one of the most common gold denominations in Elizabethan England (named for the image of St. Michael the Archangel on its face). A 'legion' invokes a Roman military unit of thousands, so Falstaff is saying Ford has thousands of gold coins. The double meaning — heavenly beings and hard cash — is the whole point: Falstaff has found a man rich enough to be worth seducing his wife.

The pun on 'angel' (coin) / 'angel' (celestial being) is a standard Elizabethan joke, used in several of the plays (e.g., Comedy of Errors 4.3: 'I see the jewel best enamelled / Will lose his beauty'). Pistol immediately picks it up: 'As many devils entertain' — countering angels with devils in the same monetary-theological register. The word 'legion' echoes the biblical phrase (Mark 5:9, the possessed man's 'My name is Legion, for we are many'), adding a further sardonic twist to the pile of coins.

anchor_text: she is a region in Guiana, all gold and bounty
summary: Guiana (in northern South America) was the location of 'El Dorado,' a legendary city of gold that English explorers were obsessively seeking in the 1590s. Sir Walter Raleigh's expedition of 1595, and his book The Discoverie of the Large, Rich, and Bewtiful Empyre of Guiana (1596), had made Guiana a byword for fabulous wealth just waiting to be exploited. Falstaff compares Mistress Ford and Mistress Page to this golden territory — to be 'traded to' for profit, not for love.
detail: Raleigh's Discoverie (1596) described Guiana as so rich that even the commonest soil glittered with gold dust, and presented the 'large, rich, and beautiful empire' as England's for the taking. The image was still culturally fresh at the time the play was written (c. 1597). By picturing two married Englishwomen as colonial territories to be exploited — 'my East and West Indies, and I will trade to them both' — Falstaff's language reveals his scheme as naked commercial extraction dressed up as courtship. The conflation of female body, foreign land, and exploitable resource was a standard metaphor in Elizabethan colonial discourse.

anchor_text: Shall I Sir Pandarus of Troy become
summary: Pandarus was the uncle of Cressida in the medieval Troy legend (Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde) who arranged the lovers' secret meetings — and whose name entered English as 'pander,' meaning a go-between for illicit sex. Pistol is refusing to carry Falstaff's love-letters on the grounds that doing so would make him a pimp. The phrase 'wear steel' (carry a sword) signals that a soldier degrades himself by acting as a procurer.

'pander': to act as a go-between for illicit sexual intercourse; from the proper name, current from at least 1526). In Troilus and Cressida (written c. 1601-2, only a few years after Merry Wives), Shakespeare's own Pandarus ends the play addressing all 'brokers-between,' knowing his name is now synonymous with procuring. Pistol's refusal to 'become' Pandarus — preferring the sword to the love-letter — is a soldier's point of honour, even from a man whose honour is otherwise flexible.

anchor_text: gourd and fullam holds, And high and low beguile the rich and poor
summary: 'Gourd' and 'fullam' are names for types of loaded dice used to cheat at gambling. 'High' and 'low' are two grades of the same fraud: 'high men' were dice loaded to throw high numbers, 'low men' to throw low. Pistol is saying that dishonesty and loaded dice profit the swindler while Falstaff takes the money and runs — and while Pistol himself will have a tester (a sixpenny coin) when Falstaff is broke again.

anchor_text: possess him with yellowness, for the revolt of mine is dangerous
summary: 'Yellowness' is Nym's term for jealousy — yellow was the color conventionally associated with jealousy and envy in Elizabethan writing (compare 'the green-eyed monster' for jealousy in Othello). Nym plans to 'possess' (fill, infect) Master Page with jealous suspicion of his wife. 'The revolt of mine is dangerous' means 'my turning against Falstaff is a dangerous thing' — a typically tangled piece of Nym's 'humour'-speak.
detail: Yellow and green were both associated with jealousy in the period, the distinction being subtle: yellow connected to bile (jealousy as a humor), green to the eye of envy. 'Humour' throughout this scene is Nym's tic-word: he applies the word to almost every noun and situation, a parody of the Jonsonian 'comedy of humours' fashion (Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour, in which Shakespeare reportedly acted, was performed in 1598). Nym's 'humour' is not quite the medical-humoral term (though it shadows that meaning) but rather a fashionable word for mood, disposition, or whim that he deploys as an all-purpose intensifier. The phrase 'my true humour' at the end of the speech is self-parody: Nym's deepest nature is apparently revenge delivered in incomprehensible syntax.

anchor_text: abusing of God's patience and the King's English
summary: To 'abuse the King's English' is to mangle the language — here Mistress Quickly anticipates that Doctor Caius's violent temper, mixed with his broken French-accented speech, will produce a spectacle of mangled oaths and grammar if he catches an unexpected visitor. The phrase was already proverbial in the 1590s. The joke is fitting: Caius speaks comically imperfect English throughout.
detail: The joke lands because Caius himself perpetually abuses the King's English — 'vat,' 'de,' 'by gar' — so Quickly's warning that he will 'abuse' it lands with extra irony. The phrase 'King's English' (referring to the standard of educated speech) appears in several Tudor texts and is recorded in Wilson, The Arte of Rhetorique (1553), which praises plain unaffected English over inkhorn terms. In the Folio (1623) the phrase is indeed 'the King's English,' consistent with a probable composition date around 1597 during Elizabeth's reign — editors sometimes note the Queen's English would be technically correct, but the reading has never been emended.

anchor_text: a posset for't soon at night, in faith, at the latter end of a sea-coal fire
summary: A posset was a hot bedtime drink made from hot milk curdled with wine or ale, taken as a comfort or a medicine. A 'sea-coal fire' burned coal shipped by sea from Newcastle to London (as opposed to charcoal or wood), which produced an intensely hot, long-lasting fire suitable for keeping a pot simmering late into the evening. Mistress Quickly is promising Rugby a warm reward — a nightcap by the dying embers — for keeping watch.
detail: Possets were associated with sick-rooms, cold nights, and domestic comfort; they appear frequently in Shakespeare as tokens of care (Macbeth's grooms are drugged with a posset). 'Sea-coal' distinguishes the fuel from cheaper or less efficient alternatives; the phrase signals a prosperous middling household. The detail grounds the scene in the everyday domestic world of Windsor.

anchor_text: he would have been horn-mad
summary: 'Horn-mad' literally meant as furious as a goring bull, but in Elizabethan usage it carried a second meaning: the fury of a cuckold — a man whose wife has been unfaithful — who was said to grow invisible horns. Mistress Quickly says Caius would have been 'horn-mad' to find a young man hidden in his house. The double meaning is typical of the play's running horn/cuckold jokes: Caius is not married, but the association of horns with male sexual humiliation colours the line.

Here it surfaces in a throwaway phrase but reinforces the pervasive anxiety about male sexual honour that Caius shares with Ford. See the reference card on the cuckold's horns.

anchor_text: ma foi, il fait fort chaud. Je m'en vais a la cour-- la grande affaire
summary: Doctor Caius breaks into French: 'ma foi' = 'my faith / good heavens'; 'il fait fort chaud' = 'it is very hot'; 'je m'en vais a la cour' = 'I am going to the court'; 'la grande affaire' = 'the great matter / important business.' He is complaining about the heat and declaring he is off to court on important business. These asides establish him as a real doctor of high social standing who actually moves in courtly circles.
detail: Doctor Caius is thought to have been modelled on the real John Caius (1510-1573), the eminent physician who co-refounded Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and served as personal physician to Edward VI, Mary I, and Elizabeth I. If Shakespeare had a real original in mind, his trips to 'de court' would glance at the actual historical figure's courtly prominence. However, the name Caius may also simply signal a learned, Latinate profession (John Caius Latinized his own name from John Kees).

anchor_text: Od's me! Qu'ay j'oublie? Dere is some simples in my closet
summary: 'Od's me' is a mild oath — 'God save me' or 'Good God' — with 'God' softened to 'Od' to avoid outright blasphemy, as the 1606 Act to Restrain Abuses of Players prohibited profane use of God's name on stage. 'Qu'ay j'oublié?' = French for 'What have I forgotten?' Caius suddenly remembers he has left medicines ('simples' — medicinal herbs or ingredients) in his closet, and rushes back — with disastrous results since Simple is hidden there.
detail: 'Simples' were single medicinal herbs or ingredients as opposed to compound medicines; a physician's 'simples' were his stock-in-trade. The closet (a small private room or cabinet for valuables and professional materials) was the standard place to keep them. The word 'simple' against the character-name Simple creates a moment of visual wordplay when Caius finds the servant among his medicines.

anchor_text: be not so phlegmatic
summary: Mistress Quickly almost certainly means 'choleric' (hot-tempered, fiery) but says 'phlegmatic' by mistake. In the theory of the four humours that governed Elizabethan medicine and psychology, phlegm was the cold, slow, calm humour — the exact opposite of the furious temper she is trying to describe. The blunder is a 'malapropism' — using the wrong word because it sounds educated — and is typical of Quickly's pattern throughout the play.
detail: Caius is a physician, so medical vocabulary is especially ironic in his housekeeper's mouth. 'Choleric' (from yellow bile, the hot angry humour) would be the correct word for Caius's furious disposition. Quickly's habit of using impressive-sounding words incorrectly is her recurring comic trait in this play, comparable to Dogberry's malapropisms in Much Ado About Nothing. The theory of the four humours (blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy) was the standard medical framework of the period, derived from Galen and widely current in popular form.

anchor_text: by gar, it is a shallenge: I will cut his troat in de Park
summary: 'By gar' is Caius's version of 'by God,' his characteristic French-accented oath throughout the play. A 'shallenge' is his rendering of 'challenge' — a formal written demand for a duel. Caius has written a letter challenging Parson Evans to a sword-fight in Windsor Park for daring to meddle in his courtship of Anne Page. The duel-challenge was a recognizable social ritual in Elizabethan England, though Shakespeare mocks its pretensions throughout.
detail: The comic force of the challenge depends on the gap between the deadly seriousness of a formal duelling culture and Caius's fractured delivery. Formal duels — governed by codes drawn from Italian fencing manuals such as Vincentio Saviolo's His Practise (1595) — were a controversial feature of Elizabethan life, condemned by authorities but widely practised among gentlemen. The duel between Caius and Evans is eventually defused by the Host, who sends them to different meeting-places as a prank. 'By gar' phonetically represents a French speaker's avoidance of 'Dieu' (God) in an oath, using a truncated form.

anchor_text: I will cut all his two stones; by gar, he shall not have a stone to throw at his dog
summary: 'Stones' was Elizabethan slang for testicles. Caius threatens to castrate Parson Evans ('cut all his two stones') and then mocks the result with a pun: a castrated man would 'not have a stone to throw at his dog.' The phrase 'not a stone to throw at a dog' was a common proverbial expression for being utterly penniless or destitute, but here it is literally true in an obscene sense.

The Winter's Tale 2.1: 'He has a lady...; and that she / Should from encounter guard') and the proverbial pebble for throwing. Caius's threat against Evans thus becomes both a violent literal castration-threat and a proverbial expression of total ruin. The comedy is characteristic of the play's bawdy register, which tends toward physical farce rather than the more elaborate wordplay of the festive comedies.

anchor_text: mine host of de Jartiere to measure our weapon
summary: 'De Jartiere' is Caius's French pronunciation of 'the Garter' — he is referring to the Host of the Garter Inn, where Falstaff lodges and where much of the play's action is arranged. The Garter Inn is the play's social hub. In 1597, the year The Merry Wives of Windsor is thought to have been first performed, Windsor was the seat of the Order of the Garter, England's highest order of chivalry, and the inn's name places the play squarely in the royal town of Windsor.

'Measure our weapon' means to have the Host settle the duel by measuring the combatants' rapiers to confirm equal length — a standard pre-duel ceremony that the Host will later subvert entirely by sending each man to a different field.

anchor_text: Love use Reason for his precisian
summary: A 'precisian' was Elizabethan slang for a strict Puritan who follows rules to the letter. Falstaff's letter says Love keeps Reason on staff as a bookkeeper ('precisian') but does not consult him as an actual adviser — in other words, love is not governed by common sense.

Using it here lets Falstaff joke that Reason is merely love's prim accountant, hired for appearance's sake but given no real authority — a way of flattering Mistress Page by suggesting that rational objections to his suit simply do not count.

anchor_text: What a Herod of Jewry is this
summary: Herod the Great, king of Judaea, was the proverbial byword for murderous ranting villainy on the English stage — old mystery plays showed him as a blustering, violent tyrant. Mistress Page uses the name to mean: 'What an outrageous bully.' Shakespeare jokes about Herod's stage rant in Hamlet ('it out-Herods Herod').
detail: Herod Antipas appears in Matthew 2 as the king who ordered the massacre of the innocents; in medieval mystery-play tradition he was always staged as a furiously ranting villain (Hamlet mocks actors who 'out-Herod Herod,' 3.2). His specific name 'of Jewry' (the Roman province of Judaea) was the common English stage formula. Mistress Page's explosion of outrage — at an old, supposedly respectable knight making love to a respectable married woman — is heightened by the hyperbole: she compares him to the most melodramatic villain in the popular theatrical repertoire.

anchor_text: the Hundredth Psalm to the tune of 'Greensleeves'
summary: Psalm 100 ('Make a joyful noise') was one of the most familiar psalm-tunes in English Protestant worship, sung by the whole congregation at a solemn, stately pace. 'Greensleeves' was a popular, bawdy dance tune of the era. Mistress Ford means that Falstaff's pious words and his lecherous intentions go together as absurdly as singing a church psalm to a tavern dance melody.
detail: The pairing is a precise comic image of hypocrisy: the Old Hundredth, as it was known, was the most broadly known metrical psalm in the Elizabethan English church, the kind sung gravely by godly congregations. 'Greensleeves' (first registered 1580) was a rousing secular tune traditionally associated with loose women and erotic play; Shakespeare mentions it twice in Merry Wives, and 'Greensleeves' may have been cant for a promiscuous woman. Forcing the two together means the tune destroys the dignity of the words — or vice versa — a perfect metaphor for the mismatch between Falstaff's moral-sounding speech and his actual purpose.

sources.name: Naylor, Shakespeare and Music
sources.citation: Naylor, Edward W., Shakespeare and Music (London: Dent, 1896), pp. 86-87 (the Old Hundredth; Greensleeves in Merry Wives).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 504

Naylor's Shakespeare and Music (London: Dent, 1896) is a real and recognized musicological source; it covers both the Old Hundredth and Greensleeves in Merry Wives, and the 1580 Stationers' Register date for Greensleeves is confirmed.
The comic pairing of a solemn psalm-tune with a bawdy dance air as an image of mismatch between Falstaff's words and intentions is exactly what the text requires (TLN 500-504).

anchor_text: lie under Mount Pelion
summary: Mount Pelion is a mountain in Thessaly, Greece. In Greek myth the Giants tried to storm Olympus by piling Mount Ossa on Mount Pelion. To 'lie under Mount Pelion' means to be crushed by an enormous weight. Mistress Page is saying she would rather suffer that impossible burden than let Falstaff press her into his printing (a bawdy double meaning on 'press' runs just before this).
detail: Ovid tells how the Giants heaped mountains upon each other to assault the gods: 'in caelum tergeminus conatus Olympum / exstruere et summo Pelion addere Olympo' (Metamorphoses 1.152-153). By Shakespeare's time the image of stacked mountains was a common classical hyperbole for anything impossibly heavy or overwhelming. The bawdy force of the surrounding passage — Falstaff 'puts us two into the press,' meaning both a printing press and a sexual imposition — makes Mistress Page's preference for being crushed under a mountain over submitting to Falstaff pointed.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.152-154 (the Giants pile Ossa on Pelion to assault Olympus); Golding trans. 1567.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 516

Ovid Metamorphoses 1.151-154 (not 152-154 as cited) does describe the Giants piling mountains toward heaven with Pelion and Ossa; the line numbers are off by one but the passage is real and supports the claim.

The bawdy double meaning on 'press' (TLN 514-515) and the hyperbolic preference for being crushed under a mythological mountain are clearly present in the text; the mythological summary (Ossa/Pelion/Olympus confusion) is imprecise but does not undermine the reading.

anchor_text: Hope is a curtal dog in some affairs
summary: A 'curtal' dog is one with its tail docked short — the tail being the visible sign of a dog's eagerness and reliability. Pistol is saying that hope is like a worthless, mutilated hound: it cannot run the full course or be trusted to bring in the prey. In plain English: hoping Ford's wife is faithful may be a poor bet.

anchor_text: He loves the gallimaufry
summary: A 'gallimaufry' (also spelled 'gallimaulfry') was a culinary word for a hash or hodgepodge of leftover meats thrown together without discrimination. Pistol uses it contemptuously: Falstaff has no standards, he pursues any woman regardless of age, rank, or looks — he loves the jumble.

anchor_text: With liver burning hot: prevent, or go thou, Like Sir Actaeon he
summary: The liver was thought to be the seat of sexual passion, so 'liver burning hot' means Falstaff is consumed by lust. 'Sir Actaeon' refers to Actaeon, the hunter in Greek myth whom the goddess Diana turned into a stag as punishment for seeing her bathing naked; his own hounds then tore him apart. Pistol warns Ford that if he does nothing, he will be like the cuckolded Actaeon — made a horned stag, hunted in his own home.
detail: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (3.138-252, trans. Golding 1567) Actaeon stumbles upon Diana bathing, is transformed into a stag, and is killed by his own dogs. 'Ringwood' (next line) was a stock English name for a hunting hound, reinforcing the image of the master become prey. The liver as the organ of lust is Galenic physiology: medieval and early modern anatomy held that the liver produced blood warm with the passions. The two ideas combine: Falstaff's 'burning liver' turns him into a hunter who will make Ford the stag. The joke is also cuckold-centred — Actaeon's stag grows horns, the universal badge of the betrayed husband.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.138-252 (Actaeon transformed by Diana); Golding trans. 1567.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 545

The liver-as-seat-of-lust is standard Galenic physiology, the Actaeon/cuckold equation is mainstream, and 'Ringwood' (TLN 546) as a hound name textually confirms the hunting conceit; the detail's reversal (Falstaff is the hunter, Ford risks becoming the stag/cuckold) correctly reads Pistol's warning.

anchor_text: ere summer comes, or cuckoo birds do sing
summary: The cuckoo's call ('cuckoo') was a homophone of 'cuckold,' the standard Elizabethan name for a husband whose wife is unfaithful. Pistol's warning is therefore a pun: take care before the cuckoo sings — meaning both 'before spring arrives' and 'before you are made a cuckold.' The same pun appears in Love's Labour's Lost 5.2 ('The cuckoo then, on every tree, / Mocks married men').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 551

The cuckoo/cuckold pun is thoroughly established in Elizabethan usage and the Love's Labour's Lost parallel is accurate; the double temporal/sexual warning suits Pistol's rhetorical style.

anchor_text: I like not the humour of lying
summary: 'Humour' here (and throughout Nym's speeches) is his tic-word, used loosely to mean 'mood,' 'habit,' 'inclination,' or simply as filler. He repeats it five times in seven lines. This is a satire on the fashionable 1590s craze for 'humour' talk, mocked in Ben Jonson's Every Man in his Humour (1598, a play Nym is borrowed from). In Renaissance medicine the four 'humours' were bodily fluids thought to govern personality; Nym applies the word to almost any situation.
detail: The comedy of humours held that a person dominated by one bodily fluid (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) was locked into a corresponding personality type. By the late 1590s 'humour' had spread from medical vocabulary into general slang for any mood or whim, a fad that satirists like Jonson targeted. Nym (whose name means 'steal' in thieves' cant) was carried over from Henry V, where he uses 'humour' the same way. He always justifies himself or ends a speech with 'and there's the humour of it' — a verbal tic that lets him sound more philosophical than he is.

sources.name: Jonson, Every Man in his Humour
sources.citation: Ben Jonson, Every Man in his Humour (first performed 1598): the comedy whose title and method directly parody the humour-talk fad that Nym embodies.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 555
Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour was first performed in September 1598, confirming the cited date; the annotation's framing of it as a satire on the humour-talk fad is accurate.

Nym uses 'humour' five times in TLN 555-561 exactly as the annotation claims, and the satire on 1590s humour-talk fad is the standard scholarly reading; the Every Man in His Humour cross-reference is appropriate.

anchor_text: I will not believe such a Cataian
summary: A 'Cataian' (or Cathayan) literally meant an inhabitant of Cathay (China), which was proverbially remote and unknown. On the Elizabethan stage the word was used contemptuously for a rogue or cheat — someone as outlandish and untrustworthy as a foreigner from the far end of the world. Page is calling Pistol an impostor not worth believing.

anchor_text: bully-rook! Thou'rt a gentleman. Cavaliero-justice
summary: The Host of the Garter speaks in a private, blustering cant. 'Bully-rook' is his boisterous term of address for a good fellow or boon companion — 'rook' from the rook (the crow family, associated with bluster), 'bully' being Elizabethan slang for a fine fellow. 'Cavaliero' (from Spanish 'caballero,' a horseman-gentleman) adds a swaggering Spanish touch, meaning a gallant man-about-town — here applied to Justice Shallow to inflate his dignity.

anchor_text: a pottle of burnt sack to give me recourse to him
summary: A 'pottle' was a half-gallon measure (two quarts). 'Sack' was a strong Spanish white wine (sherry-style), and 'burnt sack' was sack warmed and spiced — a popular Elizabethan hot drink. Ford is offering the Host half a gallon of spiced wine as a bribe in exchange for an introduction to Falstaff under the false name 'Brook.'

anchor_text: thou shalt have egress and regress; said I well
summary: 'Egress and regress' is a legal phrase meaning the right to enter and exit — used in property law for rights of access over another person's land. The Host applies it pompously to Ford's request for an introduction to Falstaff, inflating a simple favour with a lawyer's formula. The self-satisfied 'said I well?' is his habit of fishing for applause.

anchor_text: distance, your passes, stoccadoes
summary: These are technical terms from the fashionable Italian style of fencing that swept England in the 1590s. 'Distance' is the controlled gap between opponents; a 'pass' is a forward thrust or lunge; a 'stoccado' (from Italian 'stoccata') is a straight thrusting blow with the point. Shallow dismisses them all as newfangled nonsense — real men fought with the old English 'long sword,' not these Italian tricks.
detail: The Italian rapier-and-dagger style, introduced through masters like Vincentio Saviolo (whose 1595 manual Shakespeare likely knew), was controversial in England: old-school gentlemen like Shallow regarded it as foreign and cowardly compared to the blunt sword-and-buckler work of their youth. Shallow's boast that with his long sword he could make 'four tall fellows skip like rats' repeats the same joke Shakespeare gives Mercutio in Romeo and Juliet (2.4), where Tybalt's Italian technique is mocked. 'Stoccado' appears also in the Merry Wives itself at 2.3 (Caius's challenge language), giving Caius's fussy duelling vocabulary the same comic-foreign colouring.

sources.name: Saviolo, His Practise (1595)
sources.citation: Vincentio Saviolo, His Practise (London, 1595) — the principal manual of Italian rapier-fencing circulating in London; 'stoccado,' 'passa,' and 'distanza' are its core vocabulary.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 622

Vincentio Saviolo's His Practise (London, 1595) is a real publication by a real Italian fencing master resident in London, and 'stoccado,' 'pass,' and 'distance' are confirmed core vocabulary of that manual.

Shallow's contempt for Italian fencing terms (TLN 621-624) contrasted with his nostalgic long-sword boast is the obvious reading, and the Saviolo connection and Romeo and Juliet parallel are mainstream scholarly glosses.

anchor_text: the world's mine oyster, Which I with sword will open
summary: Pistol coins what became a proverbial phrase: the world is like a sealed oyster shell, and he will force it open at sword-point to get his share of wealth. It is a boast about seizing opportunity by force, not by earning it.
detail: The image is Pistol's self-aggrandising response to Falstaff's refusal to lend him money. Oysters were prised open with a knife; substituting a sword turns petty theft into mock-heroic bravado. The phrase passed almost immediately into proverbial use and is the earliest recorded instance of 'the world is your oyster' (OED, 'oyster', n., 4).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'oyster', n., sense 4: 'the world is one's oyster,' citing this passage as the earliest recorded use.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 634

The gloss is sound: Pistol's line is a boast about seizing wealth by force, the sword substituting for the knife that opens the shell, and this is the accepted earliest recorded use of the proverbial phrase.

anchor_text: retort the sum in equipage
summary: Pistol says he will 'pay back' the money in stolen goods: 'retort' means return or repay, and 'equipage' means equipment or kit, but here it is a grandiose word for plunder or petty pilfering.
detail: 'Retort' in the sense of 'return' or 'repay' is archaic (OED, 'retort', v., sense 1). 'Equipage' normally meant a set of travelling equipment or personal gear; Pistol uses it as a pompous euphemism for stolen trifles, consistent with his habit of dressing small crimes in heroic language.

anchor_text: you should lay my countenance to pawn
summary: Falstaff says he allowed Pistol to pledge his (Falstaff's) reputation as security, as if it were an object put in a pawnshop. 'Countenance' means face, appearance, and by extension social standing or credit; to 'lay it to pawn' means to borrow money using it as collateral.
detail: The image of a great knight's prestige as pawnable property is part of the play's running joke about Falstaff's poverty and pretension. He has been 'grating' (cadging) from friends on the strength of his name, effectively trading his social credit for cash.

anchor_text: looked through the grate, like a geminy of baboons
summary: Falstaff says Pistol and Nym would have been in prison, staring out through the bars like a pair of baboons. 'Geminy' (also spelled 'gemini') means a pair or couple. The grate is the barred window of a jail cell.
detail: 'Geminy' derives from Latin 'gemini' (twins); Shakespeare uses it to mean simply 'a pair' (OED, s.v. 'geminy'). The image of two ruffians peering out of prison bars like caged monkeys is a deliberate insult to Pistol's pretensions to honour.

anchor_text: to your manor of Picht-hatch
summary: Falstaff dismisses Pistol to 'Pickt-hatch,' a real London street in Clerkenwell notorious as a district of brothels and thieves' dens. Sarcastically calling it a 'manor' mocks Pistol's pretensions to gentility: his true home is the criminal underworld.
detail: Pickt-hatch (spelled variously) was a well-known disreputable quarter in the London suburb of Clerkenwell, associated with prostitution and low crime throughout the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Several contemporary writers name it as shorthand for the London underworld; Falstaff's 'manor of Picht-hatch' is a bitter joke at Pistol's expense, suggesting his only estate is a slum.

anchor_text: fain to shuffle, to hedge, and to lurch
summary: Falstaff admits he is sometimes forced to cheat, evade, and pilfer: 'shuffle' means to use tricks or act dishonestly; 'hedge' means to avoid commitment or take a crooked path; 'lurch' means to steal or rob (not its modern meaning of lurking or stumbling).
detail: All three verbs describe the compromises Falstaff makes to survive. 'Lurch' in the sense of 'to rob or cheat' was common in the period (OED, s.v. 'lurch', v.2, sense 2). The confession is self-serving: if even a knight of Falstaff's standing is forced to these stratagems, how absurd is Pistol, a common soldier, to claim a higher honour?

anchor_text: your cat-a-mountain looks, your red-lattice phrases
summary: Falstaff mocks Pistol's wild, fierce expression ('cat-a-mountain' = wildcat or mountain cat, a byword for feral ferocity) and his 'red-lattice phrases' — the slang of a tavern (alehouse signs were painted with a red lattice), that is, low drinking-house swagger dressed up as soldierly bluster.
detail: 'Cat-a-mountain' (also 'cat of the mountain') meant a wildcat or leopard; the phrase described a ferocious or uncontrollable person (OED, s.v. 'cat-a-mountain'). Red lattices were the painted window-frames used as signs for alehouses; 'red-lattice phrases' are the coarse idiom of the tavern, beneath a man of genuine honour.

anchor_text: into such a canaries as 'tis wonderful
summary: Mistress Quickly's malapropism for 'quandary': she means Falstaff has thrown Mistress Ford into such a fluster that it is remarkable. Quickly is the play's great mangler of language, and 'canaries' for 'quandary' is a typical slip.

The Canary Islands were known for a lively dance called the 'canary,' so 'in a canaries' could also mean 'in a spin' or 'all of a flutter' — either reading suits Quickly's meaning.

anchor_text: in such alligant terms
summary: Another Quickly malapropism: she means 'elegant' but says 'alligant.' The slip is typical of her character — she reaches for impressive vocabulary and misses.

anchor_text: twenty angels given me this morning; but I defy all angels
summary: Quickly has been bribed with twenty 'angels' — gold coins — by one of the suitors (almost certainly Falstaff), but then pivots to insist she 'defies' all angels in any dishonest sense. The word-play on 'angel' as both coin and heavenly messenger lets her claim virtue while admitting she has taken money.
detail: An 'angel' was an English gold coin worth about ten shillings, stamped with the archangel Michael slaying the dragon. It circulated widely in the late sixteenth century (OED, s.v. 'angel', n., sense 4). Quickly's verbal dodge — 'I defy all angels, in any such sort... but in the way of honesty' — uses the double meaning to perform innocence: she is not bribed by divine messengers of vice, only by honest gold. The pun is accidental on her part, which makes it funnier.

anchor_text: there has been earls, nay, which is more, pensioners
summary: Quickly claims Mistress Ford has turned away even the Queen's Gentlemen Pensioners — the elite royal bodyguard made up of the tallest, handsomest young men of good family. 'Pensioners' are these royal attendants, ranked above earls in desirability because they were the best-looking young men at court.
detail: The Gentlemen Pensioners (formally the Band of Gentlemen Pensioners) were the sovereign's ceremonial bodyguard, drawn from the gentry and well known for their height and fine appearance. Titania in A Midsummer Night's Dream compares her fairy attendants to 'the cowslips tall her pensioners be' for their grand looks. Quickly's claim that not even earls or the queen's own handsome pensioners could turn Mistress Ford's head is hyperbolic flattery.

anchor_text: Like a fair house built on another man's ground; so that I have lost my edifice by mistaking the place

anchor_text: damned Epicurean rascal
summary: Ford calls Falstaff an 'Epicurean rascal' — in popular Elizabethan use, 'Epicurean' meant a glutton and pleasure-seeker who lived only for bodily enjoyment, not the philosophical Epicurean ideal of moderate contentment. It is a moral insult, not a compliment.

anchor_text: Wittol!--Cuckold! the devil himself hath not such a name

anchor_text: foin, to see thee traverse; to see thee here, to see thee there; to see thee pass thy punto, thy stock, thy reverse, thy distance, thy montant

anchor_text: knowledge in Hibbocrates and Galen

'Hibbocrates' is Evans's Welsh rendering of 'Hippocrates,' keeping the joke on his accent while making the scholarly allusion clear.

anchor_text: am I a Machiavel? Shall I lose my doctor
summary: The Host boasts of his cleverness by asking 'am I a Machiavel?' — meaning a cold, scheming, amoral strategist. Marlowe's Prologue in The Jew of Malta (c. 1589) personifies 'Machevil' speaking the prologue. The Host's self-comparison is comic: he is a small-time innkeeper, and his 'policy' amounts to sending two quarrellers to the wrong fields.

anchor_text: divulge Page himself for a secure and wilful Actaeon
summary: Actaeon was a hunter in Greek myth who accidentally saw the goddess Diana bathing; she punished him by turning him into a stag, and his own hounds tore him apart. Because a stag has horns, 'Actaeon' became Elizabethan slang for a cuckold — a man whose wife is unfaithful. Ford, believing the worst, plans to expose Page as a foolish, willing cuckold who lets his wife stray.

'Secure' here means carelessly confident, unsuspecting — an ironic thrust, since it is Ford, not Page, who is the jealous husband in the play. Ford's use of 'Actaeon' is a classic Elizabethan double move: it invokes both the classical myth of a man destroyed by what he inadvertently sees AND the cuckold-horn convention, the horned stag being the badge of a deceived husband. The irony is sharp: Ford, maddened by imagined jealousy, plans to humiliate a neighbour whose wife is actually faithful, while his own wife is also being falsely suspected.

anchor_text: he kept company with the wild Prince and Pointz
summary: The 'wild Prince' is Prince Hal — the future Henry V — whose misspent youth in London taverns with lowlife companions was a favourite legend. Poins (here spelled 'Pointz') is Hal's closest drinking crony in Shakespeare's two Henry IV plays. Page objects to Fenton because he ran with this disreputable crowd before drifting to Windsor, and because he is 'of too high a region' (too grand a social rank) and presumably too expensive to marry a citizen's daughter.
detail: Shakespeare had dramatized Prince Hal's wild years in 1 and 2 Henry IV (c. 1596-98), plays almost certainly performed before Merry Wives was written (c. 1597-1602). The reference makes Fenton a figure from that world, someone who has hung around the court and its margins and spent beyond his means — 'of no having' (no fortune). Page's complaint that Fenton 'knows too much' probably means he has seen too much of the great world and has sophisticated habits Page cannot afford. The allusion also quietly signals that Fenton, unlike the foolish Slender or the comic Caius, is a genuine gentleman with a history — which is part of what makes him the right husband for Anne in the play's own terms.

anchor_text: 'Have I caught thee, my heavenly jewel?'
summary: Falstaff quotes the opening line of the Second Song from Sir Philip Sidney's sonnet sequence Astrophil and Stella (1591): 'Have I caught my heavenly jewel?' Sidney's anguished lover steals a kiss from the sleeping Stella; Falstaff borrows the most celebrated love-lyric of the era and turns it into a predatory exclamation. The quotation marks the gap between genuine passion and Falstaff's mercenary desire.
detail: Sidney's Astrophil and Stella (108 sonnets and 11 songs) was the defining Elizabethan sonnet sequence, circulating in manuscript before its posthumous print publication in 1591; by the mid-1590s its phrases were common cultural currency. The line opens its Second Song, in which Astrophil bends over the sleeping Stella. Falstaff's appropriation is both comic and damning: the lover's helpless longing is transmuted into a self-satisfied hunter's cry, and the 'heavenly jewel' he has 'caught' is a bourgeois housewife whose purse he is after. The quotation is the play's clearest signal that Falstaff is performing a role stolen from a better play.

anchor_text: love to walk by the Counter-gate, which is as hateful to me as the reek of a lime-kiln

Falstaff's comparison manages to slander Mistress Page while inadvertently advertising his own familiarity with the debtor's prison.

anchor_text: This is fery fantastical humours and jealousies. By gar, 'tis no the fashion of France
summary: Evans's 'fery' is his Welsh-accented 'very' — in Welsh English, 'v' was often pronounced as 'f.' Doctor Caius's 'By gar' is his French oath, a minced form of 'By God' ('par Dieu'). Their comic distance from English domestic culture makes them inadvertent moral commentators: Ford's behaviour looks bizarre to both a Welshman and a Frenchman.

The comedic function is dual: they raise laughs at the foreigners' expense while also allowing them to voice a detached perspective on English absurdity that a native character could not quite own.

anchor_text: the peaking cornuto her husband
summary: 'Peaking' means sneaking or skulking — moving about furtively. 'Cornuto' is Italian for 'horned one', a term for a cuckold (a man whose wife is unfaithful), derived from the traditional image of invisible horns growing from a deceived husband's head. Falstaff is calling Ford a sneaking, jealous cuckold — not knowing he is speaking to Ford himself in disguise.
detail: The irony is compounding: Falstaff describes Ford as a cuckold ('cornuto') and as jealous while reporting all this to Ford disguised as 'Brook'. The word 'cornuto' circulated as a fashionable Italian insult in Elizabethan London; Iago uses it in Othello (4.1). 'Peaking' (= peeking, sneaking) is also attested in its modern sense by 1600. The cuckold-horn tradition is ancient, running from Roman comedy through medieval fabliaux.

anchor_text: conveyed me into a buck-basket
summary: A buck-basket was a large wicker basket used to carry dirty linen to be 'bucked' — soaked in a lye solution made from wood-ash and water as part of the Elizabethan laundry process. The word has no connection to male deer; 'buck' here comes from the Old English/German word for the lye wash itself. The basket was typically full of soiled shirts, smocks, and stockings, which is exactly what Falstaff was rammed in with.
detail: Bucking was the standard pre-industrial method of bleaching and cleaning linen. The household lye was poured repeatedly through the cloth in the basket, then the clothes were beaten and rinsed. Because bucking was done in batches, the basket accumulated days of soiled linen — hence the 'rankest compound of villainous smell' Falstaff describes. The basket would have been large enough to hold a person, which is what makes the hiding-place plausible on stage.

anchor_text: like a good bilbo in the circumference of a peck, hilt to point, heel to head
summary: A 'bilbo' is a long, extremely flexible sword made in Bilbao, Spain, celebrated for its ability to bend into a circle without breaking. A 'peck' is a dry measure equal to two gallons — a roughly circular container. Falstaff is picturing himself curled inside the laundry basket like one of those bent swords, folded head to heel into the tightest possible space. The comparison is precise and comic: even a renowned flexible blade would barely fit.
detail: Bilbao blades were proverbially pliable — ships' captains entering Spanish ports were sometimes imprisoned in 'bilboes', iron shackles made from the same flexible Bilbao iron. The detail is elaborately physical: Falstaff catalogues his own compression ('hilt to point, heel to head') to maximise the humiliation and the absurdity, given that he is famously enormous. The peck-as-container (a grain measure, roughly cylindrical) gives the audience an exact image.

anchor_text: a man of my kidney, think of that, that am as subject to heat as butter
summary: 'Kidney' here means temperament or constitution — 'a man of my kidney' means a man of my kind or character. The word comes from Elizabethan humoral medicine, where the kidneys were thought to generate bodily heat and determine a person's nature. Falstaff uses it to stress that he, being a particularly hot-tempered (and fat, and sweating) person, was in special danger of melting in the hot laundry basket.
detail: The humoral body understood personality as determined by the balance of four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. The kidneys were associated with the production of warmth. 'Of his kidney' (meaning 'of his sort') appears in this play and in Henry IV Part 2. Falstaff then immediately confirms his own hot nature: he is 'as subject to heat as butter' — a substance that melts at the slightest warmth — and was 'stewed in grease' in the basket.

anchor_text: I will be thrown into Etna, as I have been into Thames
summary: Etna (now Etna) is the large active volcano on the island of Sicily. The classical tradition, following Virgil and others, placed Vulcan's forge inside it and associated it with fire, brimstone, and spectacular eruption. Falstaff uses it as the most extreme image of a fiery death imaginable — he would accept being thrown into a live volcano before he gives up his pursuit of Mistress Ford.
detail: Virgil describes the Cyclopes working under Etna at Vulcan's forge in Aeneid 8.416–25. Ovid adds the giant Typhoeus pinned under the mountain (Metamorphoses 5.346–58), whose restless thrashing causes eruptions. By Shakespeare's time Etna was the stock classical emblem of volcanic fire; its pairing with the Thames (cold, wet, English) makes the comic hyperbole symmetrically absurd — Falstaff has survived water and will survive fire.

Etna as the supreme classical emblem of fire (via Virgil and Ovid) is mainstream and defensible; the Thames/Etna water-fire symmetry that the annotation identifies is exactly the rhetorical structure Falstaff uses, and nothing here is an over-reading.

Ford, now knowing Falstaff is at his house right now, mutters this to himself: his own honour has been compromised, and his jealous schemes have made things worse. He is alone on stage and talking himself into action.

anchor_text: if I have horns to make one mad, let the proverb go with me; I'll be horn-mad
summary: Ford is playing on two senses of 'horn-mad'. The primary meaning is the rage of a cuckold ('horns' was the standard Elizabethan emblem of a man whose wife was unfaithful — invisible horns were said to grow on his head). The secondary meaning is simply as mad as a horned bull or a cornered stag — dangerously, charging mad. Ford accepts both: if he is to be a cuckold, at least let him be raging with it.
detail: The phrase 'horn-mad' appears in The Comedy of Errors 5.1 with the same double sense. The horn/cuckold motif is pervasive in Merry Wives: Falstaff literally wears a buck's horns at Herne's Oak in 5.5, which is the play's culminating visual joke. Ford's closing pun ('horn-mad') echoes his earlier, obsessive cuckold-fear and leaves him rushing on stage as a self-fulfilling jealous husband.

anchor_text: ask him some questions in his accidence
summary: 'Accidence' is the elementary branch of Latin grammar covering the basic inflections of nouns, adjectives, and verbs — what an Elizabethan schoolboy had to memorize before anything else. Mistress Page is asking Evans to test whether William has kept up with his grammar-school drills.
detail: The word comes from the Latin accidentia, 'accidents' — the variable endings that attach to a word's fixed stem to show number, case, and gender. Lily's Grammar, the authorized Tudor schoolbook, opened with the accidence. Scholars note the irony that what follows is a demonstration of how thoroughly the accidence can be misunderstood, both by Evans (whose accent distorts the paradigms) and by Quickly (who hears only English indecency).
