anchor_text: What is 'fair,' William?
summary: Evans asks for the Latin word for 'fair' or 'beautiful'; William correctly answers 'pulcher.' Quickly hears it as 'polecats' — Elizabethan slang for prostitutes. The mishearing is the first of several in the scene where standard Latin grammar is converted by Quickly's ear into sexual insult.
detail: 'Polecat' (Mustela putorius) was already slang for a loose woman in Shakespeare's England, appearing in the same sense in The Merry Wives itself (4.2) and in Cymbeline. The Latin adjective pulcher (beautiful, handsome) is one of the paradigm words in Lily's Grammar. Quickly's indignant 'There are fairer things than polecats, sure' shows she genuinely mishears, rather than making a deliberate joke — which makes the comedy richer, since the audience catches what she does not. This is the first note in the scene's sustained chord of Latin-as-bawdy.

anchor_text: focative case, William
summary: Evans's Welsh accent turns 'vocative' into 'focative' — the case used when addressing someone directly. He then says the vocative 'is caret' (Latin 'it is lacking', the standard grammar-book note that a form has no distinct ending here). Quickly hears 'focative' as an obscenity and 'caret' as 'carrot', a phallic vegetable, prompting her 'And that's a good root.'
detail: In Latin grammar, 'caret' means 'it is wanting' or 'is lacking' — a standard annotation in paradigm tables when a form has no distinct inflected ending (here the vocative and nominative are identical). Evans is teaching correctly, however mangled his pronunciation. His substitution of 'f' for 'v' is a well-attested feature of stage-Welsh English; the same swap appears elsewhere in his speeches. Quickly's 'good root' completes the bawdy sequence: 'carrot' as a root vegetable is being heard as a phallic image. The triple pun (focative / f-word; caret / carrot / root) is the scene's densest cluster of innuendo.

anchor_text: horum, harum, horum
summary: William recites the genitive plural of the Latin pronoun hic/haec/hoc: 'horum, harum, horum.' Quickly hears 'harum' as 'whore-'em' and the phrase 'genitive case' as 'Jenny's case' ('Jenny' was a common name for a prostitute), then accuses Evans of teaching the child to 'hick and hack' — Elizabethan slang for sexual activity. All three mishearings pile onto the same Latin paradigm.
detail: Horum, harum, horum is a genuine Latin paradigm from Lily's Grammar (genitive plural: of these [masc.], of these [fem.], of these [neuter]). 'Harum' was close enough to 'whore' to trigger the pun; 'horum' gives Quickly the exclamation 'fie upon you!' directly. 'Hick and hack' is glossed by Onions as of uncertain meaning with an indelicate (sexual) reference, and editors have long heard a sexual undercurrent in Quickly's line. 'Jenny' as a female name was commonly attached to a woman of loose character in Elizabethan English. Evans's exasperated correction ('art thou lunatics? Hast thou no understandings for thy cases, and the numbers of the genders?') is itself unintentionally comic.

anchor_text: you must be preeches
summary: 'Preeches' is Evans's Welsh-accented pronunciation of 'breeches' — the tight knee-length trousers worn by Elizabethan men and boys. He means William will be beaten across the backside (i.e., flogged on his breeches), a standard schoolroom punishment for a child who forgot his lesson. The threat is comic rather than alarming in context.
detail: Corporal punishment — typically caning or switching on the palm or buttocks — was routine in Elizabethan grammar schools. Evans substitutes 'pr' for 'br' as part of his Welsh phonology (the same voice that gives him 'prain' for 'brain' at TLN 1533). The threat neatly rounds off the scene: William has forgotten his pronouns, and the penalty is the schoolmaster's stick.

anchor_text: obsequious in your love, and I profess requital
summary: 'Obsequious' here means devoted or compliant, not the modern sense of groveling sycophancy. 'Requital' means repayment in kind — Falstaff promises to match Mistress Ford's supposed love with equal devotion, down to the last detail ('to a hair's breadth').
detail: Shakespeare uses 'obsequious' in its Latin root sense of 'compliant, dutiful' (from obsequor, to comply with) — the modern overtone of fawning servility is a later narrowing of the word. 'Requital' (from 'requite') meant the act of paying back; the phrase 'profess requital' = 'declare I will return it in full.' The elaborate courtly diction is itself part of the joke: Falstaff, fat and mercenary, speaks like a Petrarchan lover.

anchor_text: He's a-birding, sweet Sir John
summary: 'A-birding' means out hunting birds, typically with a hawk or with a fowling-piece (a light shotgun). Mistress Ford reassures Falstaff her husband is safely occupied away from home — which will shortly prove cruelly ironic when Ford returns moments later.

anchor_text: your husband is in his old lunes again
summary: 'Lunes' means fits of lunacy or wild raving moods. Mistress Page is telling Mistress Ford that her jealous husband has worked himself into another frenzy. The word comes from 'luna' (moon), reflecting the old belief that the moon caused madness.

'His old lunes' implies this is a recurring pattern, not the first time Ford has erupted into jealous hysteria — Ford is a known quantity in the neighborhood, his jealousy a standing joke. The word is used similarly in The Winter's Tale (3.2) of Leontes's jealous rage.

anchor_text: curses all Eve's daughters, of what complexion soever
summary: 'Eve's daughters' means all women, tracing every woman's ancestry back to Eve, the first woman of Genesis. Ford's jealousy has generalized into a rage against womankind as a whole. The phrase implies women inherit Eve's supposed capacity for deception.

In Elizabethan misogynist rhetoric 'daughter of Eve' was shorthand for a woman prone to cunning and disobedience. 'Of what complexion soever' means regardless of temperament or appearance — Ford's fury is totalizing, without exception.

anchor_text: buffets himself on the forehead, crying 'Peer out, peer out!'
summary: Ford is hitting his own forehead and shouting 'Peer out!' — commanding the invisible cuckold's horns he imagines growing there to show themselves. The action makes his jealousy both comic and pathetic: he believes he is a cuckold and beats his own head as if trying to find the horns.
detail: The cuckold's invisible horns were a fixed joke in Elizabethan England: a man whose wife was unfaithful was said to grow horns on his forehead that everyone could see except him. Ford, convinced his wife is betraying him, enacts the fantasy literally — striking himself where the horns would sprout. The gesture is a piece of visual comedy that would get an immediate laugh from an Elizabethan audience who knew the cuckold-horn convention instantly.

anchor_text: he hath an abstract for the remembrance of such places, and goes to them by his note
summary: An 'abstract' is a list or summary — Mistress Ford says her husband keeps a written inventory of every possible hiding place in the house and checks it systematically. 'By his note' means by his written list. Ford's jealousy has become organized and methodical, which makes the comedy darker and funnier.
detail: The word 'abstract' in early modern English could mean an abridgment, index, or summary document — a precursor to the modern sense. The passage paints Ford as a man who has turned domestic jealousy into an administrative procedure: he catalogs the press (wardrobe), coffer, chest, trunk, well, and vault as known hiding places and visits each in turn. This systematic mania underscores his comic obsession.

anchor_text: her thrummed hat, and her muffler too
summary: A 'thrummed hat' is one made of or fringed with thrums — short threads or tassels of yarn left over from weaving, stitched onto a fabric to create a shaggy, tufted surface. Combined with a 'muffler' (a cloth wrapped around the lower face and neck), the disguise is meant to hide Falstaff's face entirely — the hat above, the muffler below, leaving little visible.
detail: Thrummed fabric was associated with lower-class and working women's dress — the shagginess of the hat marks the 'old woman of Brentford' as a shabby, rustic type. The muffler was a common garment for women in cold or public situations, wrapping around the chin and jaw. Together they form a practical disguise, but Evans spots the flaw at TLN 1715-1716: a 'great peard' (beard) showing under the muffler gives Falstaff away.

anchor_text: 'Still swine eats all the draff.'
summary: Mistress Page quotes an Elizabethan proverb: 'draff' is swill or hogwash — the liquid refuse from brewing, fed to pigs. The proverb means the quiet pig gets all the food: those who make no noise get the most benefit. Mistress Page applies it to herself and Mistress Ford — apparently merry and harmless, they are in fact the ones who have eaten up the advantage over Falstaff.
detail: The proverb is recorded by John Heywood, A Dialogue of Proverbs (1546): 'the still sow eats up all the draff.' It worked as a self-description by the wives: people who assumed that 'merry' women were loose women underestimated them — like the quiet pig, the merry wife eats the swill while others are distracted. The rhyming couplet (TLN 1648-1651) frames the wives' moral directly: honesty and mirth are not opposites.

sources.citation: John Heywood, A Dialogue Conteyning the Number in Effect of all the Prouerbes in the Englishe Tongue (1546), Part 2, ch. 5: 'the still sow eates vp all the draffe.'

The proverb is accurately cited from Heywood (1546) and the definition of 'draff' as brewing refuse is correct; the application to the wives as apparently harmless but actually most effective is a well-supported reading of Mistress Page's self-commentary.

anchor_text: panderly rascals! there's a knot, a ging, a pack, a conspiracy
summary: 'Panderly' means pimping, acting as a go-between for an adulterous affair (from 'pander,' a procurer). 'Ging' (or 'gang') means a crew or company. Ford accuses his own servants of being part of a conspiracy to help Falstaff reach his wife, piling up near-synonyms — knot, ging, pack, conspiracy — as his rage escalates.
detail: The word 'pander' derives ultimately from Pandarus, the go-between in the story of Troilus and Cressida, whose name had become a common noun for a procurer by the late 16th century. Ford's accusation that his servants are 'panderly rascals' frames the domestic comedy in the terms of sexual betrayal. The rhetorical heaping of synonyms ('a knot, a ging, a pack, a conspiracy') is Ford at his most manic and comic — he sees a grand plot where there is only farce.

'Panderly' from 'pander' (ultimately Pandarus) and 'ging' as a crew or gang are accurate; the observation that Ford's heaping of synonyms reflects his manic state is a sound rhetorical observation well supported by the text.

anchor_text: 'As jealous as Ford, that searched a hollow walnut for his wife's leman.'
summary: A 'leman' is an archaic word for a sweetheart or lover (usually illicit). Ford is inviting the company to mock him as proverbially foolish if they find nothing again — a man who searched a hollow walnut for his wife's secret lover. The image captures how absurdly small a space Ford imagines his rival might occupy.
detail: The word 'leman' (from Old English 'leofman,' dear person) was already old-fashioned and poetic in Shakespeare's time — its use here is slightly self-mocking, giving Ford's rhetorical vow a slightly archaic, ballad-like coloring. The phrase 'searched a hollow walnut' is Ford's own self-constructed proverb of stupidity: a walnut is too small to hide a man, which underlines that Ford knows how ridiculous he looks, yet cannot stop himself.

anchor_text: A witch, a quean, an old cozening quean! Have I not forbid her my house?
summary: A 'quean' (not 'queen') meant a bold, disreputable woman or hussy; 'cozening' means cheating or swindling by deceit. Ford believes the woman of Brentford is a fraudster who works by 'charms, by spells, by the figure' (TLN 1702) — meaning by magic rituals and astrology — to swindle gullible people.
detail: 'Quean' and 'queen' were homophones but entirely different words — the distinction mattered. 'The figure' at TLN 1702 refers to a horoscope or astrological figure cast to divine the future, a standard tool of the Elizabethan 'cunning man' or 'wise woman.' Ford's linking of fortune-telling and witchcraft reflects genuine early modern suspicion of such practitioners: the Witchcraft Acts of 1563 and 1604 both targeted not just malicious witchcraft but also 'conjurations, enchantments, and sorceries' including fortune-telling.

anchor_text: Come, Mother Prat; come, give me your hand.
summary: Mistress Page improvises the name 'Mother Prat' for Falstaff's female disguise. Ford immediately picks up the pun: 'I'll prat her' — meaning 'I'll beat her backside,' since 'prat' was slang for the buttocks. The name itself announces the beating that follows.
detail: Ford's retort, 'I'll prat her,' plays on both the name and the slang term: 'to prat' meant to strike on the prat (buttocks). The joke sets up the entrance of Falstaff disguised as an old woman, who is immediately beaten as Ford 'prattles her' out the door. The name-as-joke is in the tradition of transparent comic naming — Mistress Page's choice of 'Prat' is a signal to the audience (and perhaps to Ford) even before a blow is struck.

anchor_text: I like not when a 'oman has a great peard; I spy a great peard under her muffler
summary: Sir Hugh Evans, the Welsh parson, pronounces 'woman' as ''oman' and 'beard' as 'peard' — his Welsh accent substituting 'p' for 'b' (Welsh has no /b/ in the same position). He spots the flaw in Falstaff's disguise: a large beard showing under the muffler. Evans's dialect is part of the play's comedy of regional English, but his observation here is also the key plot point that unmasks the disguise.
detail: Welsh speakers in Shakespeare's time characteristically voiced stops differently from English speakers, producing the comic substitution of 'p' for 'b' and 'f' for 'v' that Evans's speech consistently shows throughout the play. Ironically it is Evans — played for dialect laughs throughout — who is sharp-eyed enough to notice the one detail that should have exposed Falstaff to Ford. The stage business of a beard peeking out from under the muffler is both visually funny and a reminder that disguise in Elizabethan theater was always a convention the audience was in on.

The phonological explanation of Welsh 'p' for English 'b' (and 'f' for 'v') as reflected in Evans's speech throughout the play is accurate and documented; the irony that Evans, played for dialect laughs, is the one to spot the unmasking detail is a defensible and standard reading.

anchor_text: if I cry out thus upon no trail, never trust me when I open again
summary: Ford is using hunting language: a hound 'opens' (gives cry) when it picks up a scent, and follows a 'trail' (the scent track of the quarry). Ford is saying: if this hunt turns up nothing, never believe me when I give the alarm again. The irony is that he is right — Falstaff is in the house — but is about to be beaten out the door before Ford can catch him.
detail: The falconry and hunting vocabulary that runs through the play concentrates here: 'cry out upon no trail' blends the image of a hound crying on a cold or non-existent scent-line with Ford's literal investigation of his own house. 'Open' as a technical term for a hunting dog's bay when it finds or follows a scent is recorded by the period's hunting manuals and is used several times in Shakespeare (e.g. A Midsummer Night's Dream 4.1, the hounds that 'open'd and pursued'). Ford is both the hunter and, in the comedy's logic, the deceived husband who is himself the quarry of the wives' plot.

anchor_text: if the devil have him not in fee-simple, with fine and recovery, he will never
summary: Mistress Page applies the language of land law to Falstaff's moral estate: a 'fee-simple' was the most complete form of freehold land ownership, absolute and heritable; a 'fine and recovery' was a legal procedure to clear encumbrances and confirm title. If the devil does not already own Falstaff outright — title clear, no encumbrances — Falstaff will not attempt them again.
detail: In Elizabethan conveyancing, a 'fine and recovery' (technically: a 'common recovery') was a court action used to bar entails and secure an indefeasible fee-simple title to land. Mistress Page's joke is precise legal wit: the devil holds Falstaff's soul in fee-simple — the strongest possible tenure, permanent and unconditional — with the title confirmed by fine and recovery so that no future claimant (say, repentance) can recover it. 'In the way of waste' continues the legal metaphor: 'waste' in property law meant the deterioration or misuse of land by a tenant in a way that damaged the landlord's interest — here, Falstaff's lecherous 'wasting' of himself against the wives. Shakespeare uses legal language for comic hyperbole throughout the play.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1728

The legal definitions of 'fee-simple', 'fine and recovery' (common recovery as a barring of entail), and 'waste' (tenant damage to a landlord's property interest) are all accurate; the reading of the devil holding Falstaff's soul in the strongest possible tenure is a sound and precise piece of legal-comic wit fully consistent with the passage.

anchor_text: Germans desire to have three of your horses
summary: The sham-German horse-theft is Shakespeare's joke at Frederick I, Duke of Württemberg, who visited England in 1592, pressured Elizabeth I for the Order of the Garter, and finally received it in 1597. Contemporary accounts report that German visitors in his entourage were involved in horse-dealing disputes at English inns. The Host's Germans borrow his horses and vanish — puncturing the pompous foreigner who claimed royal connections.
detail: Frederick had been pestering Elizabeth for the Garter since his 1592 visit; the comedy, almost certainly composed or revised around 1597-1600, would have made the 'Duke' gag immediately recognizable. Evans and Caius explicitly mention 'the Duke de Jarmany' (4.5) and 'un gentilhomme... a German' (4.5); the Host's horses disappear and he is left credulous and cheated, mirroring the broader play theme of self-important outsiders humiliated by Windsor locals. The Folio text's 'Cotsall' variant and the Quarto's 'Garmombles' (possibly a mangling of 'Württemberg') reinforce the topical identification. Scholars identify this as a burst of timely satire rather than essential plot: the horse-theft is introduced here and resolved off-stage, serving chiefly to punish the Host who earlier tricked Evans and Caius.

sources.name: Crane / Quarto variants; Merry Wives scholarship
sources.citation: Leslie Hotson, Shakespeare versus Shallow (Boston: Little, Brown, 1931), pp. 111-28, on Frederick of Württemberg and the horse-theft allusion; see also H. J. Oliver, ed., The Merry Wives of Windsor, Arden Shakespeare (London: Methuen, 1971), Introduction, pp. xlii-xlvii.

The Frederick of Württemberg identification is the mainstream editorial consensus (Hotson, Oliver, Melchiori), the Quarto 'Garmombles' variant and 4.5 references to 'Duke de Jarmany' support it, and the reading of the scene as punishing the Host for his earlier prank on Evans and Caius is standard — medium confidence is appropriate given the circumstantial evidence.

anchor_text: I'll sauce them
summary: 'Sauce' here means to make someone pay an exorbitant price — to charge them through the nose in revenge for the trouble they have caused. The Host plans to recoup his losses by inflating the bill before the Germans can leave.

The core gloss ('charge dearly, punish financially') is textually correct and OED-supported; the summary slightly misframes the timing (the Host says 'They shall have my horses' — he is not withholding them as leverage — but the saucing-as-inflated-bill reading is sound and the minor framing slip does not distort the meaning.

anchor_text: had my house a week at command

anchor_text: They must come off
summary: 'Come off' is an Elizabethan financial idiom meaning to pay up, to settle an account, to hand over money owed. The Host insists the Germans will have to pay before they get the horses — and he intends to make the reckoning steep.

anchor_text: I rather will suspect the sun with cold
summary: Ford is swearing an oath by adynaton — declaring an impossible thing as proof of his conviction. He will sooner believe the sun is cold (a thing impossible by nature) than believe his wife is unfaithful. The speech marks his complete reversal from the jealous husband of the earlier acts.
detail: The adynaton ('impossible thing') was a recognised rhetorical device of emphasis; Elizabethan audiences would recognise the form from popular poetry and preaching. Ford's choice of the sun as his impossible test case is apt: the sun was the emblem of constancy and of truth made visible, qualities he had wrongly denied his wife. His phrase 'In him that was of late an heretic' — i.e. Ford himself, a man who doubted the true faith of his wife's honour — turns the figure toward the language of religious conversion, framing his jealousy as a kind of doctrinal error now recanted.

The adynaton reading is sound: 'I rather will suspect the sun with cold / Than thee with wantonness' is a textbook impossible-comparison oath, and the detail note's observation that heretic/faith language reframes jealousy as doctrinal error is a mainstream interpretive move well supported by the lines.

anchor_text: There is an old tale goes that Herne the hunter, Sometime a keeper here in Windsor Forest
summary: Mistress Page introduces the legend of Herne the Hunter: a former royal gamekeeper in Windsor Forest who, by local tradition, hanged himself on an oak and now haunts it at midnight in winter, wearing great antlers, rattling a chain, blasting trees, and causing cattle to give blood instead of milk. Shakespeare's play is the earliest surviving record of the legend.
detail: The 'keeper' was a forest officer responsible for managing deer and enforcing the king's hunting rights — a real role in Windsor Great Park, crown property. Whether the legend was genuinely current in Windsor or largely Shakespeare's invention is unknown; no earlier written source exists. The 'ragg'd horns' (antlers) and the blighting of cattle are stock attributes of a malevolent ghost in Elizabethan folk belief. 'Blasts the tree' means strikes it with sudden blight or death — the same word used for the Devil's breath in Hamlet (1.1). 'Milch-kine yield blood' — dairy cows giving blood instead of milk — was a standard sign of supernatural interference with livestock in early modern English witchcraft beliefs (Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft, 1584, Book 5).

sources.name: Windsor folklore; The Merry Wives of Windsor 4.4 (earliest surviving record)
sources.citation: Mistress Page tells the legend at The Merry Wives of Windsor 4.4: 'There is an old tale goes that Herne the Hunter, / Sometime a keeper here in Windsor forest, / Doth all the winter-time, at still midnight, / Walk round about an oak, with great ragged horns.' The play is the earliest known reference.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1773

Describing Merry Wives as the earliest surviving record of the Herne legend is accurate and widely accepted; the characterisation of the keeper role and the attribution of cattle-blighting to standard Elizabethan ghost belief are defensible, and the gloss does not overclaim a definite historical origin for the legend.

anchor_text: The superstitious idle-headed eld Received, and did deliver to our age

anchor_text: Disguis'd, like Herne, with huge horns on his head
summary: The plan is for Falstaff to wear the antlered head of the ghost-hunter Herne. The joke is layered: Falstaff came to Windsor hoping to make Ford a cuckold (the man whose wife is unfaithful was said to grow invisible horns), and now he himself is made to wear real horns — the hunter becomes the hunted, and the would-be seducer is marked with the badge of shame he wanted to plant on others.
detail: The converging of the literal deer-antlers (Herne the ghost-hunter) with the figurative cuckold's horns is the comic pay-off the play has been building since Act 1. In 5.5 Falstaff himself will acknowledge it: 'I do begin to perceive that I am made an ass' and 'a Windsor stag, and the fattest, I think, i' the forest.' The Actaeon myth (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3) shadows the device: Actaeon the hunter was transformed into a horned stag and destroyed — the hunter hunted. Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) also describes horn-wearing folk customs at midwinter revels.

sources.name: Elizabethan proverbial lore; Ovid, Metamorphoses 3 (Actaeon)
sources.citation: The horned cuckold was a fixed joke of Elizabethan English; its mythic emblem is Actaeon, turned into a horned stag (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.138-252, Golding 1567). Cf. The Merry Wives of Windsor 5.5.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1789

Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.138–252 (Actaeon's transformation to a horned stag and destruction) and Golding's 1567 English translation are both confirmed real sources that support the cuckold-horns / hunter-hunted claim.

The convergence of Herne's literal antlers with the figurative cuckold's horns is the play's central comic conceit, supported by Falstaff's own acknowledgement in 5.5; the Actaeon parallel (hunter-hunted) is a well-established reading, not an overreach, given Falstaff's self-description as a stag in 5.5.

anchor_text: Like urchins, ouphs, and fairies, green and white
summary: 'Urchins' in Elizabethan English could mean hedgehogs, but more often meant goblins or mischievous sprites thought to take hedgehog form. 'Ouphs' (also spelled 'oafs') are elves or fairy changelings — the word is cognate with 'oaf,' originally a fairy's dull, clumsy substitute left in a stolen child's place. Green and white were conventional fairy colours in Elizabethan folk belief.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'urchin' n.: a goblin or mischievous sprite (sometimes imagined in hedgehog form); s.v. 'ouph' n.: 'an elf, goblin, or fairy changeling.'

sources.name: Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584)
sources.citation: Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), Book VII (the catalogue of bugbears and night-spirits — 'bull-beggars, spirits, witches, urchins, elves... Robin Goodfellow... hobgoblin'), which lists urchins among the popular sprites.

anchor_text: I'll to him again, in name of Brook
summary: 'Brook' is the false name Ford uses when he visits Falstaff in disguise. Pretending to be a jealous stranger who wants to pay Falstaff to seduce Mistress Ford on his behalf, Ford tricks Falstaff into reporting every detail of the scheme back to the very husband he is supposedly cuckolding. The irony is that Ford, obsessed with discovering evidence of his own dishonour, is the one supplying the opportunity.

sources.name: Bate and Rasmussen, eds., Merry Wives (RSC Shakespeare)
sources.citation: Bate, Jonathan, and Eric Rasmussen, eds., The Merry Wives of Windsor, RSC Shakespeare (Basingstoke: Macmillan, 2011), introduction and notes on the 'Brook'/'Broome' textual crux.

anchor_text: Go, get us properties And tricking for our fairies
summary: 'Properties' are stage props — physical objects needed for a performance; the word was standard backstage vocabulary in Elizabethan theatre. 'Tricking' means decorative dress or ornamentation — the costumes and accessories for the children's fairy disguises. Mistress Page is directing the practical preparations as if stage-managing a play-within-the-play.
detail: The theatrical vocabulary ('properties,' 'vizards' at TLN 1819) is deliberate: the wives are staging a performance to catch Falstaff, and Shakespeare signals this by giving them the language of the tiring-house. 'Vizards' (TLN 1819) are masks. 'Tricking' derives from 'trick' in the heraldic sense of sketching or adorning an armorial device, hence elaborate, festive decoration.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'property' n., sense 14b: 'a portable article used in acting a play, a stage accessory'; s.v. 'tricking' vbl. n., sense 2: 'decoration, ornamentation, dress.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1828
OED sense 14b for 'property' as a theatrical stage accessory (attested from c. 1425) and 'tricking' as ornamentation/decoration are both genuine dictionary senses that support the glosses.

'Properties' as stage props and 'tricking' as ornamental costuming are correct period senses; the heraldic etymology for 'tricking' is accurate, and the observation that the theatrical vocabulary signals a play-within-the-play dynamic is a sound and standard reading.

anchor_text: That Slender, though well landed, is an idiot; And he my husband best of all affects
summary: Mistress Page's aside exposes the competing marriage schemes: her husband wants to marry their daughter Anne to Slender (who owns good land — 'well landed' — but is a fool), while she secretly favours Doctor Caius ('well money'd' and with powerful connections at court). Neither parent knows that Anne has already chosen Fenton for herself. 'Affects' means 'prefers' or 'is attached to.'
detail: Elizabethan marriage law gave fathers the primary legal authority over a daughter's match, but a mother's strong preference — especially in a household as harmoniously disorganised as the Pages' — could count heavily. The tension between a good estate (land = stable, inherited wealth) and money + court connections (the new Tudor economy of cash and patronage) reflects a real social division in 1590s England. Slender's 'well landed' status echoes the gentry world of the play's Windsor setting, while Caius's court connections point to a more mercenary, mobile kind of influence. The joke of the final scene is that both parents' schemes misfire and Anne chooses love over either form of social ambition.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (Berlin, 1874–75), s.v. 'affect' v., sense 1: 'to love, to be attached to, to favour.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1836

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference work and its 'affect' entry sense 1 ('to love, to be attached to, to favour') directly supports the summary's gloss of 'affects' as 'prefers' or 'is attached to.'

The gloss is accurate: 'well landed' = possessing good land holdings, 'affects' = prefers/is attached to, and the detail note's contrast between landed gentry wealth and Caius's cash-and-court-connections model correctly identifies a real late-Tudor social tension without overstating it.

anchor_text: story of the Prodigal
summary: The Host says Falstaff's chamber is decorated with a painted scene of the Prodigal Son, the parable from Luke 15 about a young man who wastes his inheritance on riotous living and ends up feeding pigs before returning home in shame. Such biblical scenes were routinely painted on the walls of inns and taverns; hanging them in the common rooms was both decoration and moral instruction.
detail: The irony is sharp: Falstaff, the play's supreme wastrel and self-indulger, lodges in a room whose walls tell the story of reckless squandering and its consequences. The Prodigal Son was one of the most frequently depicted biblical subjects in Elizabethan popular art, so the joke lands immediately. Falstaff has also been described in the Henry IV plays as a kind of corrupt Prodigal-Son figure — here the connection is made visible in the furnishings of his rented room.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Luke 15:11-32 (Geneva 1599): the son who demands his inheritance, squanders it in 'riotous living,' and returns in shame to his father's forgiveness.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1845
Geneva Bible 1599, Luke 15:11-32 uses the exact phrase 'riotous living' (Luke 15:13) and the parable runs verses 11-32 as cited; source is real and directly supports the claim.

The Host's description of Falstaff's chamber being 'painted about with the story of the Prodigal' is verbatim in the text, and the ironic parallel between the wastrel Falstaff and the Prodigal Son is mainstream-defensible; inn-room biblical paintings are well-attested in the period and the Henry IV Prodigal-Son resonance is accepted critical tradition.

anchor_text: Anthropophaginian unto thee
summary: An 'Anthropophaginian' is an eater of human flesh — a cannibal. The word is a comic inflation of 'anthropophagi,' the legendary man-eating peoples described by ancient and medieval geographers. The Host warns Simple that Falstaff may roar at him as ferociously as a cannibal; the polysyllabic monstrosity of the word is itself part of the joke.
detail: The word derives from Greek anthropos (human being) + phagein (to eat). 'Anthropophagi' appear in Othello ('the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / do grow beneath their shoulders'), where Othello cites them among the wonders of his travels. Shakespeare reaches for the term whenever a character wants to sound magnificently threatening or absurdly exotic. Here it parodies the Host's own bombastic manner of speech: he piles up synonyms ('brief, short, quick, snap') and then warns Simple about a man who might out-shout even him.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'anthropophagus': from Greek anthropophagos, 'man-eating'; used by Elizabethan writers for the legendary cannibals of remote regions (e.g. Pliny, Natural History 7.2, describing peoples 'who eat human flesh').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1847
Pliny, Natural History 7.2 does describe the Anthropophagi (man-eating Scythians) in chapter 2 of Book 7, confirming both the OED derivation claim and the classical citation.

The core gloss — an eater of human flesh, a comedic inflation for 'cannibal' — is sound and directly supported by Othello's 'Anthropophagi' parallel; the explanation that the polysyllabic monstrosity is itself the joke is the mainstream reading of the Host's bombastic idiom throughout this scene.

anchor_text: thine Ephesian, calls
summary: The Host calls himself Falstaff's 'Ephesian,' a piece of Elizabethan cant meaning a boon companion, a familiar crony, a fellow of the same drinking brotherhood. The word has nothing to do with the city of Ephesus; it was slang for a comrade in revelry.
detail: The same cant usage appears in Henry IV Part 2 (2.2), where the Prince calls his low companions 'Ephesians.' The origin of the slang is uncertain — possibly a jocular echo of the communal spirit praised by Paul in Ephesians, or simply a piece of tavern argot that had attached to the word. The Host's self-description ('it is thine host, thine Ephesian, calls') is typical of his habit of multiplying self-congratulatory titles: host, Ephesian, bully, heart-of-gold.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T. (1986). A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Eagleson. Oxford UP, s.v. 'Ephesian': 'a boon companion (cant term).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1853
Onions, Shakespeare Glossary s.v. 'Ephesian' records the cant sense 'boon companion / toper,' and the H4P2 2.2 parallel usage is confirmed.

'Ephesian' as Elizabethan cant for a boon companion is firmly attested in Onions and supported by the Henry IV Part 2 parallel; the gloss accurately notes the origin is uncertain without overclaiming.

anchor_text: Bohemian-Tartar tarries
summary: The Host calls Simple a 'Bohemian-Tartar,' stacking two words that carried identical connotations for Elizabethans: a wandering, untrustworthy outsider. 'Bohemian' in this period meant a Gypsy or vagrant (Gypsies were popularly thought to come from Bohemia or Egypt); 'Tartar' referred to the nomadic Tatar peoples of Central Asia, a byword for fierce, uncivilized wanderers. Together they are a comic way of calling Simple a vagrant nonentity.
detail: Neither term is a straightforward ethnic slur in its specific meaning here; both function as generic insults for a low-status wanderer who hangs about without invitation. The doubling ('Bohemian-Tartar') is typical of the Host's style: he heaps up words for comic effect rather than precision. Compare his earlier address to Simple: 'boor... thick-skin.' Elizabethan English used 'Bohemian,' 'Egyptian,' 'Gypsy,' and 'Tartar' more or less interchangeably for travelling outsiders.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'Bohemian' sense 2: 'A Gypsy'; and s.v. 'Tartar' sense 1b: 'A member of the combined forces of Central Asian Turkic and Mongol peoples'; used figuratively for a fierce or intractable person.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1855

OED 'Bohemian' sense 2 as 'a Gypsy' is well attested; the 'Tartar' citation conflates the literal ethnic sense with the figurative 'fierce person' sense but both appear in the OED and the overall claim is supported.

Both 'Bohemian' (vagrant / Gypsy) and 'Tartar' (fierce nomadic outsider) as generic insults for low-status wanderers are well-attested Elizabethan usages, and the reading that the Host piles them up for comic effect rather than ethnic precision fits his established speech-style in this scene.

anchor_text: wise woman of Brainford
summary: A 'wise woman' was an Elizabethan term for a local cunning-woman or folk healer: someone who located lost goods, read fortunes, identified thieves, made love-charms, and sometimes sold remedies. 'Brainford' is Brentford, a market town a few miles upriver from London on the Thames. Wise women were a well-known feature of popular culture, consulted by ordinary people for exactly the kinds of questions Slender sends Simple to ask — whether he will get the girl, who stole his chain.
detail: Legally, a wise woman occupied a grey area: she might be prosecuted under the Witchcraft Acts (1563 and 1604) if her activities caused harm, but most were tolerated as useful neighbourhood figures. In Merry Wives the 'fat woman of Brentford' is actually Falstaff in disguise (he has escaped Ford's second raid by dressing as her), but the townspeople plainly know of a real 'wise woman' from Brentford, showing Shakespeare drawing on genuine local colour rather than pure invention. Brentford was a staging-post on the road west from London, familiar to London audiences.

sources.name: Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic
sources.citation: Thomas, Keith (1971). Religion and the Decline of Magic. Weidenfeld & Nicolson, pp. 212-52 (on the role and methods of cunning folk in early modern England).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1860
Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971, Weidenfeld & Nicolson) is a real work whose Chapter 8 covers cunning folk; pages 212-252 are a plausible range for that chapter in the first edition.

The 'wise woman' as a cunning-woman / folk healer is accurately defined, and the point that townspeople know of a real Brentford wise woman (while Falstaff exploits the identity as cover) is the standard dramatic reading; the claim that Shakespeare draws on genuine local colour here is mainstream and defensible.

anchor_text: three Doctor Faustuses
summary: Bardolph compares the three German horse-thieves to 'three Doctor Faustuses' — the legendary German scholar who sold his soul to the devil for magical powers, famously dramatized in Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (c. 1592, performed through the 1590s). Marlowe's Faustus conjures, shape-shifts, and performs impossible tricks; the fleeing Germans seemed, to Bardolph, to vanish as supernaturally as Faustus. The comparison also jokes that a man willing to sell his soul might also steal three horses.
detail: The historical Faustus was a real figure — a boastful German astrologer and magician of the early sixteenth century who attracted contemporary comment — but by Shakespeare's time he was primarily a theatrical personality via Marlowe's hugely popular play, which was still being performed. For a Windsor audience the association of the German con-men with Faustus also plays on the stereotype of Germans as given to dark arts and occult learning. The 'Duke of Germany' subplot (the fake German duke who borrows horses) may glance at actual diplomatic incidents involving German visitors to the English court in the mid-1590s.

sources.name: Marlowe, Doctor Faustus
sources.citation: Christopher Marlowe, The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus (c. 1592; first printed 1604). The legend derives from Historia von D. Johann Fausten (Frankfurt, 1587), the German Faustbuch translated into English as The History of the Damnable Life and Deserved Death of Doctor John Faustus (London, 1592).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1892

Marlowe's Doctor Faustus is correctly dated to c.1592 (within the contested 1588-1593 range; Wikipedia gives 1592-93); the Faustbuch (Frankfurt, 1587) and its English translation (London, 1592) are both confirmed real publications.

Bardolph's exact words 'three Doctor Faustuses' appear at TLN 1892-1893 and the allusion to Marlowe's play as the primary reference point for the legend (rather than the chapbook) is defensible given the theatrical context; the extra claim about a German-occult stereotype is plausible colour but not overreach.

anchor_text: cozen-germans that has cozened all the hosts of Readins, of Maidenhead, of Colebrook
summary: Evans warns that three 'cozen-Germans' (a pun: cousin-Germans means first cousins; 'cozen' means to cheat) have swindled innkeepers in Reading, Maidenhead, and Colnbrook — all real towns strung along the road west from Windsor toward London on the Bath road. The episode almost certainly alludes to a real 1592 incident in which a man claiming to be a German duke's courier cheated English innkeepers out of horses.
detail: Evans's Welsh accent turns 'flouting-stocks' into 'vlouting-stogs' a few lines earlier and 'Readings' into 'Readins,' but his meaning is clear: a confidence trick is working its way up the road toward Windsor. 'Cozen-Germans' is a true pun — the thieves are strangers from Germany, but the construction also echoes 'cousin-german' (first cousin), implying an intimate familiarity that makes their betrayal of trust worse. The specific towns — Reading (10 miles south-east), Maidenhead (6 miles east), Colnbrook (10 miles east on the main London road) — place Windsor firmly in real Berkshire geography, which is the play's whole project: the first and only Shakespeare comedy set in a recognizable contemporary English town.

sources.name: Hotson, Shakespeare versus Shallow
sources.citation: Hotson, Leslie (1931). Shakespeare versus Shallow. Little, Brown, pp. 111-21 (identifying the 1592 German-duke horse-theft incident as likely background to the subplot).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1899

Hotson's Shakespeare versus Shallow (1931) exists and Little, Brown is a confirmed publisher, but the book's main thesis concerns Shallow/Gardiner and the specific pages 111-21 as the locus for the German-duke horse-theft argument cannot be verified; other standard editions (e.g. Arden) attribute that identification to different scholarship.

The 'cozen-Germans' pun on 'cousin-german' (first cousin) plus 'cozen' (cheat) is the standard editorial gloss; the identification of Reading, Maidenhead, and Colnbrook as the real road west from Windsor is accurate geography; the annotation appropriately marks the Hotson historical identification as medium-confidence.

anchor_text: gibes and vlouting-stogs
summary: Evans's Welsh accent renders 'flouting-stocks' as 'vlouting-stogs': he means the Host is full of gibes and mockeries, treating serious things as a joke. 'Flouting' means jeering or scoffing; a 'stock' here is a laughing-stock, an object of ridicule. Evans uses the phrase to say the Host is the sort of man who makes fun of everything — and therefore may not take the warning seriously enough.
detail: The Welsh substitution of 'f' for 'v' is Evans's most consistent phonetic habit (compare 'fery' for 'very,' 'Got' for 'God'). 'Flouting-stog' for 'flouting-stock' combines the verbal noun with the common suffix for a person who embodies something (like 'laughing-stock'). Evans's dialect is part of Shakespeare's larger joke about the misuse and mangling of English by learned foreigners — Evans the schoolmaster, Caius the doctor — in contrast to the native-born townspeople.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T. (1986). A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Eagleson. Oxford UP, s.v. 'flouting-stock': 'an object of scoffing or ridicule.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1902
Onions, Shakespeare Glossary s.v. 'flouting-stock' ('an object of scoffing or ridicule') is a real entry and correctly supports the annotation's gloss.

Evans's 'vlouting-stogs' for 'flouting-stocks' (laughing-stock, object of scorn) is the standard gloss; the Welsh f/v substitution is consistent throughout the play and well-documented; the reading that Evans is accusing the Host of habitual mockery fits the dramatic context of his warning being brushed aside.

anchor_text: liquor fishermen's boots with me
summary: Falstaff imagines the court laughing so hard at his humiliations that they would 'melt me out of my fat' and use the rendered grease to waterproof fishermen's boots. In this period 'to liquor' a boot meant to rub it with tallow or grease to make it waterproof — the word has nothing to do with alcohol here. Falstaff sees himself reduced to a raw material, a tub of lard good only for oiling work-boots.
detail: The comic image compounds Falstaff's self-pity: he has been dunked in dirty laundry, beaten while disguised as an old woman, and now fears public exposure at court. The fat-rendered-to-grease image returns to Falstaff's physical bulk as a constant point of humiliation throughout the play, playing on the stock comedy of his great size. 'Liquor' in the sense of rubbing with a substance survives in the modern compound 'shoe-blacking.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'liquor' v. sense 2: 'To smear, rub, or dress with grease or oil; especially, to grease (boots or leather) to make them waterproof.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1915
OED 'liquor' v. sense 2 ('to smear with grease or oil; to grease boots to make them waterproof') is a real and well-documented sense that directly supports the annotation.

The OED sense of 'to liquor' (to grease boots with tallow) is unambiguously the correct reading here — the alcohol sense is impossible given 'fishermen's boots' as the object — and the fat-to-grease self-reduction image fits Falstaff's pattern of humiliated self-description throughout this speech.

anchor_text: forswore myself at primero
summary: Primero was the fashionable card game of Tudor England, essentially a precursor to poker, played with stakes and involving bluffing and declaration of hands. 'Forswore myself' means Falstaff swore falsely — cheated, or lied about his hand. He is saying, half-seriously, that his bad luck dates from the moment he cheated at cards and broke an oath.
detail: Primero (from Spanish primera) was played at court and among gentlemen throughout the sixteenth century; Henry VIII and Elizabeth I were both known players. Each player received four cards and bet on combinations; bluffing was central. To 'forswear' oneself at cards would mean either falsely swearing the value of a hand or swearing to a wager one did not intend to pay. Falstaff's rueful linking of oath-breaking to bad fortune is a comic inversion of the moral that perjury leads to punishment — his tone suggests he thinks the punishment disproportionate to merely cheating at cards.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander (1874). Shakespeare-Lexicon, 2nd ed. Berlin, s.v. 'primero': 'a game at cards, in which four cards were dealt to each player.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1917
Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874, Berlin) is a real reference work and its description of primero as a four-card dealing game matches independent sources on the game's rules.

Primero as a fashionable Tudor card-game involving bluffing and stakes is accurately described; 'forswore myself' meaning swore falsely (cheated or lied about a hand) is the standard reading; the annotation does not overclaim in suggesting Falstaff's tone implies the punishment is disproportionate — the comic register of the speech supports this.

anchor_text: mirth whereof so larded with my matter
summary: 'Larded' is a culinary term meaning 'threaded through with fat to enrich it'; here Fenton uses it figuratively to mean the comic plot (mocking Falstaff) is so interwoven with his own serious business (marrying Anne) that the two cannot be shown separately. The word was a standard Elizabethan metaphor for mixing or enriching one thing with another.
detail: The kitchen image — larding a joint of meat with strips of fat before roasting it — was a common Elizabethan metaphor for weaving strands of discourse or story together. Fenton's point is practical: the letter from Anne describes the fairy-masque prank on Falstaff, and that context is necessary to understand how Fenton's own elopement plan is hidden inside it. He cannot explain the one without revealing the other. Shakespeare uses the verb elsewhere in the same sense of rich interweaving (e.g. Hamlet 4.5, Ophelia's song, 'Larded all with sweet flowers').

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'lard' v., the figurative sense 'to interlard, intersperse, mix' (well attested from the 16th century).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T. A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Eagleson (Oxford, 1986), s.v. 'lard': 'to intersperse, interlard.'

anchor_text: To-night at Herne's oak, just 'twixt twelve and one
summary: Herne the Hunter is a ghost of Windsor Forest — a former royal gamekeeper said to walk at midnight wearing great antlers and to blast trees and bewitch cattle. The wives have chosen his haunted oak as the site for Falstaff's humiliation because it lets them dress Falstaff in a buck's horns: the deceived would-be seducer becomes the horned ghost himself, in a forest famous for the cuckold's joke of the horns.
detail: Shakespeare is the earliest surviving source for the Herne legend; whether he invented it or drew on local Windsor tradition is unknown. The midnight hour ('twixt twelve and one') signals the ghost's time, and the disguise of Falstaff with antlers fuses two ideas the play has been developing throughout: the literal horns of the hunter-deer and the figurative 'horns' of the cuckold — the man whose wife is unfaithful. Falstaff came to Windsor to cuckold Ford and Page; at Herne's Oak he is made to wear the cuckold's badge himself. The Herne's Oak scene runs from 4.4 through 5.5 and is the play's climactic comic set-piece.

sources.name: Windsor folklore; Merry Wives 4.4
sources.citation: The Merry Wives of Windsor 4.4 (Mistress Page introduces the legend): 'There is an old tale goes that Herne the Hunter, / Sometime a keeper here in Windsor forest, / Doth all the winter-time, at still midnight, / Walk round about an oak, with great ragged horns.' The play is the earliest known record of the legend.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1955

The sole source cites MWW 4.4 for the Herne legend text, and the claim that the play is the earliest known record of the legend is supported by standard scholarship (Wikipedia, Britannica, and folklore studies all confirm Shakespeare's play is the earliest written source).

The reading is careful — it does not overclaim a pre-Shakespearean source for the Herne legend, correctly identifies the midnight hour from the text, and the antlers-as-cuckold-horns double meaning is a mainstream critical reading well supported by the play's running deer/horn/cuckold imagery.

anchor_text: other jests are something rank on foot
summary: 'Rank' here means fully grown, ripe, or in full vigorous progress — not offensive. 'On foot' means underway. Fenton is saying that while the other plots (the Falstaff prank, the rival suitors' scramble) are in full swing and occupying everyone's attention, Anne can slip away to marry him.

sources.name: OED

anchor_text: quaint in green she shall be loose enrob'd, With ribands pendent
summary: 'Quaint' here means elegantly or cunningly dressed — not 'charming' or 'old-fashioned' as it means today. Green was the conventional colour of fairies in Elizabethan tradition, and 'loose enrob'd' means clothed in a flowing, unbelted gown. 'Ribands pendent' are ribbons hanging down. Mistress Page's instruction gives Anne the appearance of a fairy, which is what will distinguish her to Doctor Caius — and what will also let her escape his notice in the dark.

Fenton's counter-plan depends on the confusion this generates. 'Quaint' in the sense of 'cleverly devised, trim, elegant' was current from Middle English through the late 16th century; its modern meaning of 'pleasingly old-fashioned' is a later narrowing.

The verbal use of 'husband' meaning to manage or conserve carefully is well-attested Elizabethan usage, and the gloss accurately captures the Host's meaning — keep the plan tightly managed and secret.

anchor_text: divinity in odd numbers, either in nativity, chance, or death
summary: Falstaff appeals to a widespread Elizabethan belief that odd numbers (especially three, seven, and nine) were lucky or sacred. The three key moments of life — birth ('nativity'), fortune ('chance'), and death — were thought to cluster around odd numbers; three was associated with the Trinity, and proverbially with lucky repetition ('third time lucky').
detail: The folk belief in the virtue of odd numbers was ancient and pan-European; it surfaces in Virgil (Eclogues 8.75: 'numero deus impare gaudet', 'God delights in the odd number') and was commonplace in Elizabethan popular culture. Falstaff's framing — nativity, chance, death — maps the odd number onto all three decisive thresholds of human life, giving his comic superstition a mock-philosophical shape. He is about to try for a third assignation with Mistress Ford, having been twice humiliated, and uses this numerological consolation to steady his nerve.

anchor_text: I'll do what I can to get you a pair of horns
summary: Mistress Quickly means the stag's antlers Falstaff will wear as part of his Herne the Hunter disguise at Windsor Forest. But 'horns' also carried an automatic secondary meaning in Elizabethan English: a cuckold — a man whose wife is unfaithful — was said to wear invisible horns. The joke here works on both levels: Falstaff will literally wear horns while playing a ghost, and figuratively, Ford is the cuckold-victim Falstaff imagines himself making.
detail: The cuckold's horns joke runs throughout the play — Ford's jealousy centers on the fear of wearing them, Falstaff's buck disguise at the end literalizes the horn imagery, and the Ford/Brook plot turns the tables so Ford is ritually humiliated before being reconciled. Mistress Quickly's throwaway line here plants the punning motif just before the final scene's convergence.

anchor_text: in the Park about midnight, at Herne's oak
summary: Herne's Oak was a real (or widely believed real) ancient oak tree in Windsor Great Park, said to be haunted by Herne the Hunter — a ghostly figure with stag's antlers who rode at night and blasted trees. The wives have told Falstaff to meet them there wearing a buck's head, exploiting the legend so that the other townspeople, coming to play fairies, will be able to terrify him without anyone suspecting the trick.

anchor_text: I fear not Goliath with a weaver's beam, because I know also life is a shuttle
summary: Falstaff packs two Bible references into one boast. Goliath's spear is described in 1 Samuel as having a shaft 'like a weaver's beam' — meaning thick as the wooden rod on a loom — to convey his monstrous size and strength. Falstaff claims he does not fear even that giant. Then he adds 'life is a shuttle': a direct echo of Job 7:6 ('My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle'), meaning life passes as quickly as the shuttle racing across a loom. Both images reach for the same prop — the weaver's loom — in consecutive breaths.
detail: The double allusion is Falstaff's characteristic mode of braggadocio built from scripture. The Goliath passage (1 Samuel 17:7) was one of the most familiar in the Geneva Bible; the 'weaver's beam' was proverbial for an impossibly large spear. Job's 'shuttle' (Job 7:6) was equally well-known as a figure for life's brevity. Falstaff's linking them is a piece of learned comic display: he claims fearlessness against a giant, then immediately admits that life is short — a quietly self-deflating admission that his boastful courage is running out of time.

anchor_text: couch i' the castle-ditch
summary: 'Couch' means to lie low and hide, not to sit on a sofa. The 'castle-ditch' is the moat or defensive ditch around Windsor Castle. Page is telling the group to conceal themselves at the edge of the moat until the mock-fairy procession lights up the park.

anchor_text: we have a nay-word how to know one another
summary: A 'nay-word' is a watchword or secret code — a phrase agreed in advance so two people can recognize each other in the dark or in disguise. Slender explains that Anne will be dressed in white; he will call out 'mum' (silence) and she will reply 'budget' (probably a corruption of the French 'bouger,' meaning 'stir' or 'move'), confirming her identity.
detail: The pair 'mum and budget' was a proverbial Elizabethan children's game or silence-keeping formula. 'Mum' meant 'be silent'; 'budget' (sometimes 'budge') meant the opposite — 'move' or 'speak up.' Together they formed a recognition ritual. Shallow immediately deflates the elaborate scheme (TLN 2020-2021): if Anne is the only one dressed in white, the code is unnecessary. His point exposes Slender's characteristic fussiness and nervousness about the whole elopement plan.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2017

The core gloss (nay-word as watchword, mum/budget as recognition pair) is sound, but calling 'budget' a corruption of French 'bouger' is a folk etymology that is contested — OED treats its origin as obscure — and the claim that the pair was a children's game goes slightly beyond what the primary sources establish; the observation about Shallow's deflating commentary is accurate and helpfully contextualizes the passage.

anchor_text: take her by the hand, away with her to the deanery
summary: A 'deanery' is the official house and jurisdiction of a cathedral dean — a senior clergyman who runs the day-to-day administration of a cathedral chapter. Windsor Castle has its own dean and a collegiate church (St George's Chapel), so Mistress Page is directing Caius to elope with Anne at that ecclesiastical office. The plan is for a quick, private marriage away from her husband's knowledge.

Mistress Page's scheme requires speed ('dispatch it quickly'), which explains why she picks a nearby church official rather than the parish. The irony the audience already senses is that Caius will be foiled: instead of the green-dressed Anne, he will end up eloping with a boy in green, and the marriage will not happen at all. OED s.v. 'deanery': 'the official residence and jurisdiction of a dean of a cathedral or collegiate church.'

anchor_text: couched in a pit hard by Herne's oak
summary: Herne the Hunter was a ghost of Windsor Forest — a former royal gamekeeper said to walk at midnight wearing great antlers, blasting trees and bewitching cattle. The wives have chosen his oak as the site of the final trick: Falstaff will be lured there disguised in a buck's head, so he wears the horns of the ghost. 'Couched' means hidden and crouching; the group is concealed nearby with their lights darkened, ready to burst out.
detail: The legend of Herne the Hunter is first recorded in this play (4.4), making Shakespeare possibly its inventor or the earliest source. By sending Falstaff to Herne's Oak with antlers on his head, the wives fold together two threads: the horned ghost of the forest and the 'cuckold's horns' joke — Falstaff came to Windsor hoping to cuckold Ford and Page, but it is he who ends up wearing the horns. 'Couched' (lying low, hidden) is hunting vocabulary, which deepens the scene's irony: the hunter Herne becomes the game, and the wives are the hunters.

sources.name: Windsor folklore; The Merry Wives of Windsor 4.4
sources.citation: Mistress Page at The Merry Wives of Windsor 4.4: 'There is an old tale goes that Herne the Hunter, / Sometime a keeper here in Windsor forest, / Doth all the winter-time, at still midnight, / Walk round about an oak, with great ragged horns.' This is the earliest surviving record of the legend.

The double-horns reading (ghost's antlers conflated with the cuckold's horns) is well-attested in scholarly commentary, the qualified framing that Shakespeare may be the legend's inventor is the correct hedged position, and 'couched' as hunting vocabulary is a defensible contextual gloss.

anchor_text: Against such lewdsters and their lechery
summary: 'Lewdster' is an Elizabethan word for a lewd or lascivious person — someone who pursues sexual misconduct. It survives only here in Shakespeare. Mistress Page is generalizing the lesson of the trick: men like Falstaff who chase married women deserve to be exposed, and the women who expose them have committed no betrayal ('no treachery') by doing so.
detail: The couplet ('Against such lewdsters and their lechery, / Those that betray them do no treachery') is a rhymed moral maxim, functioning like a sententia — a pithy general truth used to close a scene with a ringing verdict. The device was a standard rhetorical flourish in Elizabethan drama; audiences expected a well-turned couplet to sum up the moral stakes before an exit. Here it also pre-empts any criticism of the wives for their elaborate deception of Falstaff, grounding their conduct in a clear ethical claim: a cheat who sets out to seduce another man's wife has no complaint if he is gulled. The word 'lewdster' (a lewd person) is rare — Merry Wives is its best-known instance.

anchor_text: Trib, trib, fairies
summary: 'Trib, trib' is Evans's Welsh-accented rendering of 'trip, trip' — a call to move quickly and lightly. Welsh speakers in Elizabethan English comedy often reversed p and b sounds; the joke is that the disguised fairy-leader sounds nothing like a real fairy.
detail: The p/b reversal is a consistent marker of Evans's Welsh dialect throughout the play ('pribbles and prabbles', 'pold' for bold, 'pid' for bid). 'Trip' as a light, quick movement appears elsewhere in fairy contexts — compare Puck's use in A Midsummer Night's Dream. The comedy here is doubled: Evans is rallying children dressed as fairies while himself unable to speak plain English.

anchor_text: Be pold, I pray you
summary: 'Pold' is Evans's Welsh pronunciation of 'bold' — be brave, do not lose your nerve. Welsh English in this period characteristically swapped initial b and p; Shakespeare uses this consistently for Evans throughout the play as a comic marker of his foreign accent.

Elizabethan stage convention used consistent accent markers to identify comic foreigners: Evans's Welsh inversion, Doctor Caius's French substitutions ('by gar', 'vat'), and comparable devices in other plays gave audiences a quick shorthand for ethnic origin. The instruction 'be bold' is entirely sensible as a stage-direction in disguise: the children playing fairies must commit to the performance.

anchor_text: follow me into the pit
summary: 'The pit' refers to a hiding place — likely a hollow or ditch in Windsor Park — where Evans and the disguised fairies will conceal themselves until the signal to emerge and torment Falstaff. In the Elizabethan theatre the word could also carry the sense of the 'pit' of the theatre itself (the standing area below the stage), which may have prompted a knowing audience laugh as Evans leads his charges toward the groundlings. The Arden and Oxford editors treat it simply as a practical hiding place within the park.

'Pid' is Evans's Welsh pronunciation of 'bid' (told, commanded). The watchword system was standard military and theatrical practice for co-ordinating a surprise action.

The word recurs in the histories (e.g. 1 Henry IV) in actual battle contexts; here it is comically domesticated into a suburban ambush. Evans's mangling of 'bid' to 'pid' is the same p/b inversion that produces 'pold' for 'bold' and 'trib' for 'trip' earlier in these three lines.

anchor_text: Jove, thou wast a bull for thy Europa
summary: Falstaff compares himself to Jupiter (Jove), king of the gods, who transformed himself into a bull to carry off the princess Europa, and then into a swan to seduce Leda. The allusion justifies his own lust by pointing out that the greatest of gods was also driven by sexual appetite.
detail: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (2.833-875) Jupiter disguises himself as a white bull to abduct the Phoenician princess Europa, carrying her over the sea to Crete; in Book 6 (6.109) he becomes a swan to assault Leda, queen of Sparta. Falstaff's logic is deflating satire: if Jupiter stooped so low ('near the god drew to the complexion of a goose'), mortal Falstaff can hardly be blamed for chasing the wives of Windsor. The comedy layers classical grandeur onto a fat, ridiculous man standing in a park with a buck's head on.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.833-875 (Europa); 6.109 (Leda and the swan); Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2050

Ovid Met. 2.833-875 is the real Europa passage; the swan/Leda allusion appears in Arachne's tapestry at Met. 6.103-128, making '6.109' a plausible specific line within that confirmed span, and Golding's 1567 translation is real.

Falstaff's self-comparison to Jove-as-bull (Europa) and Jove-as-swan (Leda) is explicit in the text (TLN 2050-2053) and the satiric deflation — a fat, ridiculous man invoking divine precedent for lust — is the plain comic logic of the scene.

anchor_text: here a Windsor stag; and the fattest, I think, i' the forest
summary: Falstaff casts himself as a stag in rut waiting for the does. A stag's antlers are also the cuckold's horns he has come to bestow on Ford and Page, but the reversal the play delivers is that Falstaff himself ends up wearing the horns.
detail: 'Rut-time' (TLN 2059) is the mating season of deer, and 'piss my tallow' means sweat away his body-fat in sexual heat. Falstaff's self-description as the 'fattest stag in the forest' combines real physical comedy (his enormous belly) with the erotic boast. The scene's dramatic irony is pointed: the man who came to plant cuckold's horns on two husbands is himself costumed in horns and will be pinched, burned, and mocked. See also herne-the-hunter for the ghost-legend Shakespeare is exploiting.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary (Oxford, 1911; rev. R. D. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'rut-time'; 'tallow.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2058

Onions's Shakespeare Glossary (Oxford, 1911; rev. Eagleson, 1986) is a real standard reference and does cover 'rut-time' and 'tallow' as Elizabethan vocabulary; the factual claims are uncontroversial lexicography.

'Rut-time' (TLN 2059) and 'piss my tallow' make the stag-in-rut reading explicit, and the dramatic irony of the horn-bearer coming to bestow cuckold's horns is straightforwardly supported by the scene's action.

anchor_text: let the sky rain potatoes; let it thunder to the tune of 'Greensleeves'
summary: Falstaff calls for a storm of exotic aphrodisiacs. Sweet potatoes (newly imported from the Americas) and eringo (candied sea-holly root, sold by apothecaries) were both believed to act as sexual stimulants. 'Greensleeves' was a popular song of the day associated with loose women.
detail: 'Potatoes' here are sweet potatoes (Ipomoea batatas), first brought to England from the Americas via Spain in the late sixteenth century and quickly given a reputation as aphrodisiacs; ordinary potatoes were not yet common. Eringoes (sea-holly root, Eryngium maritimum) were candied and sold as a restorative and supposed stimulant. 'Kissing-comfits' are perfumed sugar-plums used to sweeten the breath before a kiss. The speech is a baroque fantasy of luxury and sensual excess, satirising Falstaff's self-delusion even as he mistakes himself for a Jovian seducer.

sources.name: Gerard, The Herball (1597)
sources.citation: John Gerard, The Herball, or Generall Historie of Plantes (London, 1597), on sweet potato and eryngo; cf. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'eringoes'; 'potato.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2062
Gerard's Herball (1597) is confirmed real and does discuss sweet potato aphrodisiac properties and eryngoes as a restorative stimulant; Onions's Glossary is a legitimate supporting reference.

Sweet potatoes and eringoes as supposed Elizabethan aphrodisiacs, and 'Greensleeves' as a song associated with loose women, are well-documented; the annotation correctly distinguishes sweet potatoes from common potatoes.

anchor_text: Divide me like a brib'd buck, each a haunch
summary: A 'bribed buck' is a deer poached or given as a bribe from a royal forest; it was customarily divided among the keeper, the woodward (forest official), and the person who received it. Falstaff offers himself — his body — to be shared out between the two wives, like an illicit carcass.
detail: Forest officers who took a bribe in the form of a deer would divide the animal by customary shares: the 'fellow of this walk' is the keeper of that section of the park. Falstaff's joke maps this carving onto a plan to sleep with both women simultaneously, promising each 'a haunch' of himself while his horns go to their husbands. The bawdy logic is grotesque: he is both the prize and the carcass.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon (Berlin, 1874-1875; 3rd ed. 1902), s.v. 'brib'd buck'; 'haunch'; 'walk.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2067

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (Berlin, 1874-75; 3rd ed. 1902) is a real standard reference; 'brib'd buck' as a deer taken illicitly from a royal forest and shared by forest officers is well-documented Elizabethan usage that Schmidt covers.

A 'bribed buck' as a deer illicitly taken from a forest and divided by customary shares is standard lexicography, and Falstaff's grotesque mapping of his own body onto that division is directly supported by the text ('each a haunch... my shoulders for the fellow of this walk').

anchor_text: my horns I bequeath your husbands
summary: Falstaff says he will 'bequeath' the cuckold's horns to Ford and Page — the invisible antlers that, in Elizabethan comic convention, a man grew when his wife was unfaithful. He came to Windsor intending to be the adulterer who puts horns on the husbands; instead he is already wearing literal horns as Herne the Hunter.
detail: The cuckold's horns were a fixed Elizabethan joke: an unfaithful wife gave her husband invisible antlers on his forehead, a mark of shame he could not see himself. Falstaff's line works on two levels: he boasts he is about to make Ford and Page cuckolds, but the audience can see he is the one already wearing the buck's head. The play's running joke reverses throughout Act 5 Scene 5 — the man who hunted wives becomes the 'hunted stag' pinched by fairies. See the-cuckolds-horns for the Actaeon mythic background.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary (Oxford, 1911; rev. R. D. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'horn'; 'cuckold.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2068
Onions's Shakespeare Glossary is real and does gloss 'horn' and 'cuckold'; the cuckold-horns convention is uncontroversial, and the reference card links are appropriate.

The double level — Falstaff boasting he will make the husbands cuckolds while himself visibly wearing the buck's head — is exactly what the text performs, and the cuckold's horns convention is well established.

anchor_text: Crier Hobgoblin, make the fairy oyes
summary: An 'oyes' (or 'oyez,' French for 'hear ye') was the formal call a court crier made to demand silence before a proclamation. Anne Page, playing the Fairy Queen, orders Pistol (playing Hobgoblin) to cry it out so the fairies fall silent. The mock-fairy court mimics the procedure of a real royal court.
detail: Court criers in English courts still open sessions with 'Oyez! Oyez! Oyez!' — a signal that an official announcement is about to be made. By having the Fairy Queen issue this command in the language of ceremony, Shakespeare makes the fairy masque a parody of courtly or legal procedure, which sits with the play's broader satire on Windsor's civic rituals. 'Hobgoblin' for Pistol connects him to the Robin Goodfellow tradition of mischievous household sprites.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'oyez' (a court crier's call to attention, from Anglo-French oiez, 'hear ye').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2083
OED s.v. 'oyez' confirming the Anglo-French court-crier formula is a real and directly supportive citation for this archaic-vocab/historical claim.
'Oyes'/'oyez' as the court crier's call for silence before a proclamation is correct, and the mock-courtly framing of the fairy masque is well supported by the scene's ceremonial diction throughout.

anchor_text: Cricket, to Windsor chimneys shalt thou leap: Where fires thou find'st unrak'd, and hearths unswept, There pinch the maids as blue as bilberry
summary: The fairy orders reflect actual Elizabethan folklore about household spirits: hearths left unswept and fires not banked ('unrak'd') at night were thought to invite the mischief of sprites such as Robin Goodfellow. Slovenly servants who failed in these duties would be pinched black and blue by the fairies — an old explanation for unexplained bruises. A 'bilberry' is a dark blue-black wild berry.
detail: Reginald Scot's The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), a primary source for Elizabethan fairy lore, records the belief that Robin Goodfellow would do household tasks if properly respected but would pinch lazy maids who neglected the fire and hearth. By assigning these punishing duties to 'Cricket,' Anne Page maps the Windsor children onto the full tradition of British hobgoblins. The scene's moralizing — good fairies reward the virtuous and punish the slovenly — frames the coming punishment of Falstaff as a cosmic settling of accounts.

sources.name: Scot, Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584)
sources.citation: Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (London, 1584), Book 7, on Robin Goodfellow and household sprites.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2085

Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) does discuss Robin Goodfellow and household fairy lore, but the pinching-maids-for-neglected-hearths detail appears in Books 3-4 (not Book 7, which covers demonic possession and conjuring charms); the 'Book 7' citation is likely incorrect, making the precise reference unverifiable without access to the full text.

The folklore that household sprites punished lazy maids who left fires unbanked and hearths unswept is documented in Scot's Discoverie (1584) and the text's language ('unrak'd,' 'unswept,' 'pinch') maps directly onto it.

anchor_text: Strew good luck, ouphes, on every sacred room
summary: 'Ouphes' (also spelled 'oafs') is an archaic word for elves or fairy children — specifically changelings left by fairies in place of human babies. Here it is simply a name for the fairy-folk ordered to bless Windsor Castle.
detail: The word 'ouphe' derives from the belief in fairy changelings: the 'oaf' or 'auf' was the dull, misshapen creature left behind when fairies stole a human child. By Shakespeare's day it could be used broadly for any fairy or elf. The line signals the shift from punishing-the-slovenly to blessing-the-noble, as the fairies move from household mischief to the ceremonial blessing of Windsor Castle and the Order of the Garter — the play's compliment to the monarch.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ouphe' (a fairy, goblin, or changeling; cf. 'oaf,' from the same root).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2099
OED s.v. 'ouphe' confirming the word as a fairy, goblin, or changeling cognate with 'oaf' is a real and directly supportive citation.

'Ouphes' as elves or fairy-folk (related to 'oaf' via changeling belief) is standard etymology, and the transition in the speech from punishing slovens to blessing Windsor Castle is clearly present in the text.

anchor_text: The several chairs of order look you scour With juice of balm and every precious flower: Each fair instalment, coat, and several crest, With loyal blazon, evermore be blest
summary: The fairies are ordered to clean and bless the 'chairs of order' — the ceremonial stalls in St George's Chapel, Windsor, assigned to each knight of the Order of the Garter. Each stall bears the knight's 'instalment' (the ceremony of installation), his 'coat' (coat of arms), and his 'crest' (heraldic device above the helm). This is a direct compliment to the Garter knights and to Queen Elizabeth.

sources.citation: Leslie Hotson, Shakespeare versus Shallow (London: Nonesuch Press, 1931), on the Order-of-the-Garter installation context proposed for the play's first performance.
